accessConditions.prerequisite: AREC2003 or RSEC2031 or ECOS2001 or ECOS2901

learningOutcomes: Apply and refine main economic theoretical concepts in formulation of problems related to non-renewable resource use
Conceptualise the relationship between economics and the environment with regards to the use of minerals, and generation and consumption of energy
Demonstrate ability to conduct a meaningful empirical economic analysis of minerals and energy related topics
Demonstrate knowledge of the business environment, industry structures and commodity and financial markets related to the minerals and energy industries
Demonstrate ablity to provide sound economic policy advice on minerals and energy issues

units.name: Economics of Water and Bioresources
units.description: This unit develops knowledge and skills in natural resource economics built on previously gained economics training. The economics of dynamic natural systems is studied through application of advanced modelling approaches. Particular emphasis is given to the economic mechanisms for managing water and biological resources including property rights, water allocation, and water markets. Key policy instruments, taxes, quotas, and standards are analysed. Institutional and policy aspects will also be considered via analysis of water policy reform in Australia and elsewhere.

accessConditions.prerequisite: AREC2003 or RSEC2031 or ECOS2001 or ECOS2901

learningOutcomes: demonstrate competency in undertaking complex dynamic economic analyses that involve renewable natural resources
demonstrate an ability for sound economic analysis related to water use and water quality
demonstrate knowledge of the most important contemporary issues related to the economics of renewable resource use and water in Australia and on the global scene
demonstrate ability to conceptualise the relationship between water economics and the role of water as a natural resource vital for the environment
produce and effectively communicate sound policy advice to policymakers that make decisions about the use of renewable resources.

units.name: Agricultural Finance and Risk
units.description: Agricultural production is typically risky, adding complexity to decision analysis and increasing need of risk consideration in agricultural policy design. This unit explores this theme, and has two related components: risk and risk management in agriculture, and issues of agricultural producer finance. These two components cover a broad range of topics that incorporate production risk and other sources of risk in agriculture.

accessConditions.prerequisite: AREC2005 or AREC2001 or AREC2002 or ECOS2001 or ECOS2901 or ECOS2040

learningOutcomes: demonstrate a sound understanding of theoretical knowledge of decision-making under risk and uncertainty in agriculture
demonstrate a sound understanding of the methods and tools for dealing with risk and uncertainty that are available to agricultural producers
demonstrate a sound understanding of different representations of risk and uncertainty
demonstrate an ability to use data to calculate different measures of risk and uncertainty
demonstrate an ability to clearly communicate results and implications of applied economic analysis.

units.name: Agricultural Production Economics
units.description: This unit of study is concerned with the application of microeconomic principles to management decisions in agricultural production systems. It builds on the theoretical knowledge acquired in previous studies and introduces the methods of applied economic analysis through a range of topics including: production, cost and profit functions; methods for the measurement of productivity; optimisation in biological production systems; and production under risk. The unit introduces the linear programming technique to solve decision making problems encountered by agribusiness and natural resource firms and managers in public agencies.

accessConditions.prerequisite: AREC2005 or ECOS2001 or ECOS2901 or AREC2003

learningOutcomes: Demonstrate ability to conceptualise production decisions made by producers
Apply production theory to empirical economic problems in agricultural, environmental and natural resource contexts
Perform basic evaluation of productivity and efficiency
Conceptualise and analyse risk and uncertainty in production economics context
Analyse production behaviour in a dynamic context
Use linear programming techniques to analyse and optimise production decisions

units.name: Benefit-Cost Analysis
units.description: Benefit-cost analysis underlies many widely used economic analysis methods, including economic impact analyses, business cases, cost-effectiveness studies, and policy evaluations. This unit covers the theory and procedures of conducting a benefit-cost analysis. Common economic analysis techniques are learned through analysing various case studies. These techniques include valuing AR market impacts like changes in employment, property values, and wages; non-market valuation methods like hedonic pricing and contingent valuation; discounting; the value of a statistical life; and sensitivity analysis.

accessConditions.prerequisite: ECOS2001 or ECOS2901 or AREC2005 or AREC2003

learningOutcomes: demonstrate an understanding of the theoretical underpinnings of benefit-­cost analysis
demonstrate development of skills and experience for undertaking practical benefit­-cost analysis studies
demonstrate an understanding of the interpretation of benefit-­cost analysis studies
demonstrate an understanding of the main techniques used in non-­market valuation
communicate complex technical information clearly and convincingly
evaluate the strengths and weaknesses of the benefit-­cost analysis methodology, including ethical implications.

units.name: Style and Substance: Introducing Art History
units.description: Taking a diverse, global view of art making from the Ancient to the Modern world, ARHT1001 will introduce students to key philosophical and methodological approaches in the field of Art History. As our experiences are increasingly mediated through a variety of visual platforms, this course will help students develop critical perspectives on visual communication. The development of professional skill sets will be a key focus. As such, the course serves as an essential introduction to Art History for those considering a career in the arts, education, or the museum and design sectors.
learningOutcomes: develop an understanding of key practices and methods of the discipline of art history
develop skills of visual literacy - the ability to analyse a work of visual art
develop new skills of critical thinking, problem solving and information literacy
develop academic and professional writing and communication skills
learn about the traditions of a wide variety of cultural groups
build confidence and resilience working with others and on self-managed projects
engage with leading organisations beyond the university and learn about their professional practices.

units.name: Shock of the Now: Global Art Since 1900
units.description: Art shapes our cities, streets, galleries, phones and minds. It is now made with every conceivable material, and sometimes none at all. It shocks, challenges, soothes, entertains, engrosses and overwhelms us. This unit charts the history of Modern and Contemporary Art across the world, as it is shaped by and shapes society, politics and environment. It shows current concerns in art , with materials, landscape, self-image, politics, and the body are grounded in a century of global experiment
learningOutcomes: demonstrate familiarity with the major trends in modern global art
identify works of art as belonging to various schools or ‘isms’
understand the dynamic inter-relations between art and society in the modern and contemporary period
use the analytical tools and conceptual grammar needed to discuss modern and contemporary art and film.

units.name: Pollock to Psychedelia
units.description: This unit studies the interplay between high art and popular culture in America from the 1950s onwards. Pop Art, Minimalism and Performance formed alongside emerging youth cultures of political protest, drugs and rock music. We examine the interactions of high art, youth culture and mass media.

accessConditions.prerequisite: 12 credit points at 1000 level in Art History or 12 credit points at 1000 level in American Studies

learningOutcomes: demonstrate and enhanced understanding of the American visual arts of the post-War period
present solid skills in writing about a suitable artwork in the Artworks review (prepared in a major gallery)
discuss key concepts for the understanding of post-War American art
construct and maintain arguments that link individual artworks to the social and political conditions of the 1950s and 1960s.

units.name: High Renaissance Art
units.description: This unit will explore a range of alternative approaches to some of the most famous works of art in the Western tradition, including works by Leonardo, Raphael, Michelangelo and Titian. Topics to be investigated include: problems of definition in High Renaissance and Mannerist art; Rome under Julius II and the creation of an imperial capital; Venetian visual poesie; art and dynastic display in Medicean Florence; civic ritual and public space; eroticism and mythology at princely courts; portraiture and gender.

accessConditions.prerequisite: 12 credit points at 1000 level in Art History or 12 credit points at 1000 level in Italian Studies

learningOutcomes: demonstrate knowledge of major artists and monuments in sixteenth-century Italy, and of the key themes, issues and critical debates around the study of High Renaissance art
demonstrate enhanced skills of visual and spatial analysis of works of art and architecture, including some of the most celebrated works in the history of Western artistic tradition
demonstrate skills of critical analysis of scholarly debates, and independent research skills.

units.name: French Art, Salon to Cezanne
units.description: This unit treats French Art in terms of the cultural structures that allowed academic art, Realism, Impressionism and Post-Impressionism to emerge. Mainstream art is studied alongside emerging avant-gardes. Other topics include nationalism, exoticism, and peripheral versus metropolitan modernism.

accessConditions.prerequisite: 12 credit points at 1000 level in Art History or 12 credit points at 1000 level in Critical Studies

learningOutcomes: To provide students with a solid understanding of the history of art produced in France between 1850–1900.
To introduce students to the key art historical skill of visual analysis through the interpretation of art.
To develop students’ verbal and written skills to interpret art in its historical and cultural context.
To engage students with current debates about the canon of French art from the Salon to the Post-Impressionism of Cézanne.
To provide a foundational knowledge base for the more advanced study of the history of art in senior level courses within the Department of Art History.

units.name: Contemporary Indigenous Art
units.description: The new has no meaning without the old, and the radical newness of the contemporary Indigenous art movement is underpinned by cultural practices dating back 50, 0000 years.Through in-depth visual analysis of individual artists and art-producing communities, you will consider the distinct Indigenous art practices and relate them to issues of cultural and political sovereignty, colonisation, lands rights and representation. Problematising the historical and contemporary reception of Indigenous art, the unit prioritises Indigenous modes of value and reflects on the deep systems of knowledge that continue to inspire artists, curators and scholars.

accessConditions.prerequisite: 12 credit points at 1000 level in Art History or 12 credit points at 1000 level in Indigenous Studies

learningOutcomes: understand the diversity of Indigenous contemporary art practice
relate contemporary art practice to issues of assimilation, colonisation, sovereignty, and reconciliation.
problematise the dichotomies between remote/urban, art/craft, ethnography/art, traditional/contemporary
be aware of the multiple regimes of value that shape the circulation of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander art in Australia and globally
demonstrate knowledge of the historical reception of Indigenous art and the shifting frameworks of Indigenous museology
engage with works of art and discuss them in relation to art historical and political interpretations of Aboriginal art
demonstrate skills in critical reading, writing, and thinking.

units.name: Art, Race and Resistance 1788-Now
units.description: This unit critically analyses the visual culture of modern imperialism and cultural histories of resistance. We engage diverse artistic practices and multiple geographies: from imperial city planning in the metropole to parodic street theatre in the colonies; from exoticized and primitivist colonial imagery to the visual culture of wars of resistance. This unit engages with post-colonial and Indigenous perspectives, critical race theory and debates about global histories of art as tools for critically analysing the visual histories of economic and territorial imperialism, as well as their contentious contemporary legacies.

accessConditions.prerequisite: 12 credit points at 1000 level in Art History

learningOutcomes: Analyse the role of visual culture in histories of empire from the 19th century to today.
Develop an historical understanding in order to respond to current debates about art and empire.
Use oral and written skills to develop visual analysis.
Clearly communicate about art and empire in oral and written tasks.

units.name: Fashion and Dress: Past and Present
units.description: This unit offers an introduction to the study of dress through the discussion of major theories and methodologies that inform current scholarship in the field. With a focus on designers, wearers and cultural practices of dressing the body, the unit will question how dress communicates as a form of visual expression.

accessConditions.prerequisite: 12 credit points at 1000 level in Art History

learningOutcomes: develop the ability to identify and discuss key theories and practices relating to the study of dress across a variety of disciplines
demonstrate a critical understanding of leading designers and designs, materials and practices
develop new skills of critical thinking, problem solving and information literacy
develop the skills to approach and discuss complex topics with sensitivity
build skills related to offering feedback to peer.

units.name: Planetary Art: Nature, Ecology, Environment
units.description: This unit studies contemporary and historical artists in relation to today's environmental crisis. Students engage with how art objects and art making relate to issues pertaining to nature, ecology, and the environment. Through visual and textual analysis, students gain interdisciplinary perspectives on art's place within contemporary posthumanist theories, the significance of ecological thinking to contemporary aesthetics, art's historical response to the impact of science and technology, and art's recognition of the importance of Indigenous knowledges to planetary ethics.

accessConditions.prerequisite: 12 credit points at 1000 level in Art History or 12 credit points at 1000 level in Critical Studies

learningOutcomes: demonstrate confidence with research skills in relation to art that engages with 'ecology' 'environment' 'nature'
demonstrate facility with critical judgment and independent thinking
demonstrate ability to plan, structure and complete well-argued writing
demonstrate skills with the visual analysis of objects and artworks
develop the analytical tools and conceptual grammar needed to discuss historical and contemporary art.

units.name: Art, Memory, and Identity
units.description: Students study contemporary and historical art in relation to collective or public memory, as well as personal memory. Memory as a subject, and memory as a tool, are considered in relation to the making of art objects and their reading. The unit looks at art's connection with the past, with history, trauma, loss and remembrance, as well as art's connection with identity, dreams, and childhood. Students gain informed perspectives on how memory is theorised as a phenomenon both real and imaginary, and why memory is often judged as more important to art than history.

accessConditions.prerequisite: 12 credit points at 1000 level in Art History

learningOutcomes: demonstrate confidence with research skills in relation to art that engages with "memory" and "identity"
demonstrate facility with critical judgment and independent thinking
demonstrate ability to plan, structure and complete well-argued writing
demonstrate skills with the visual analysis of objects and artworks
work cooperatively with others and share equally in assessment tasks
develop the analytical tools and conceptual grammar needed to discuss historical and contemporary art.

units.name: Islamic Art and Architecture
units.description: We survey the complex arts, architecture and material culture of the Islamic world and explore critical debates that help us relate different traditions that encompass this broad category of visual culture. We introduce important global, transcultural, and transregional currents in art history through an object-oriented approach to teaching that includes the on-site study of gallery and museum collections.

accessConditions.prerequisite: 12 credit points at 1000 level in Art History or 12 credit points at 1000 level in Critical Studies or 12 credit points at 1000 level in Visual Arts

learningOutcomes: recognize and analyse the arts, architecture and material culture of the Islamic world
apply skills of observation and analysis of visual materials, extending and amplifying their critical practice
exhibit skills and abilities in presenting visual material through critical argument in extended written and oral presentations
assume responsibility for their own research methods and encounter the full spectrum of methods of research and scholarship
engage with each other as peer supporters and learners through preparation, engagement and questioning in tutorials
encounter and engage a variety of global traditions of art and explore the critical debates that help relate different traditions within the broader history of art in the world.

units.name: Why Art Matters
units.description: Why Art Matters explores the importance of art in the world, through object-based seminars, lectures and student led presentations. It asks why art is so fundamental to human experience, and how we might study it and articulate its importance. It builds key art historical skills of recognition, analysis, interpretation and expression, and introduces students to a wide variety of different material objects and artworks. The course is taught in small group streams, largely in the Chau Chak Wing museum and will help all majoring art history students build confidence and skill in researching, analysing and communicating about art.

accessConditions.prerequisite: 12 credit points at 1000 level in Art History

learningOutcomes: Students encounter and engage a variety of global traditions of art and explore the critical debates that help relate different traditions within the broader history of art in the world
Students engage with objects to hone skills of observation and analysis, extending and amplifying their critical practice.
Students acquire knowledge of specific areas, periods, genres and styles of art and visual culture.
Students extend their skills and abilities in presenting visual material through critical argument in extended written and oral presentations.
Students assume responsibility for their own research methods and encounter the full spectrum of methods of research and scholarship
Students engage with each other as peer supporters and learners through preparation, engagement and questioning

units.name: Modern Art: Europe and the Islamic World
units.description: This unit explores the key role art from the Islamic world played in modern European art. It traces the impact of western art on modern visual culture across the Middle East from the nineteenth century onwards. We explore the new aesthetics of this hybrid visual culture and the cultural politics of its international dissemination, which was fuelled by art dealers and exhibitions. We discuss the cosmopolitan careers of artist-travellers and post-colonial and global theories of art by which to interpret their work. This unit’s expansive geography encompasses the cross-cultural exchanges that transformed modern eastern and western European, American, Persian, Ottoman and Australian cultures.

accessConditions.prerequisite: 12 credit points at 2000 level in Art History or (6 credit points at 2000 level in Art History and CASF1001 and CASF1002)

learningOutcomes: Deepen knowledge about the role of cross-cultural encounters in the transformation of modern European, American, Persian, Ottoman and Australian visual cultures from the nineteenth century to the present day.
Develop and refine skills of visual analysis and oral and written skills in formulating an argument about works of art.
Develop an historical understanding of debates around orientalism and Islamic art in order to engage in current debates about this topic

units.name: Australian Art and Film
units.description: What are the current debates and issues driving Australian art, film and visual culture? In interrogating present-day cultural perspectives, this unit examines, analyses and reinterprets the relationship between colonial and contemporary imagery through screenings, on-site gallery visits and the study of works held in university and other local art and film collections.

accessConditions.prerequisite: 12 credit points at 2000 level in Art History or 12 credit points at 2000 level in Film Studies or 6 credit points at 2000 level in Art History and CASF1001 and CASF1002

learningOutcomes: develop a broad understanding of key issues in Australian art, film and visual culture. They will be introduced to art historical research methods through course content and through practical processes of research and inquiry. They will learn to critically analyse and evaluate contemporary artworks in a range of media. They will acquire new knowledge through independent research, with a focus on developing independent thinking, analysis and project management.

acquire the skills and confidence to communicate their knowledge of Australian art, film and visual culture in written and verbal form. They will engage in classroom experiences that allow them recognise and value communication as a tool for negotiating and creating new understanding, interacting with others, and furthering their own learning.

develop the ability to respond effectively to unfamiliar problems in unfamiliar contexts (for instance, on site in an art gallery, or evaluating films, videos and related art works in unconventional public spaces). They will gain experience in working effectively in teams and other collaborative contexts.

develop an understanding of how to use information effectively in a range of contexts. They will recognise pertinent information needs; use appropriate media, tools and methodologies to locate, access and use information; critically evaluate the sources, values, validity and currency of information; and use information in critical thinking.

engage critically with ‘real world’ social, cultural and ethical issues through on-site seminars and through assessment tasks, and apply local and international perspectives to extend their knowledge of Australian imagery.

units.name: The Asian Modern: Art in East Asia
units.description: This unit investigates key debates about the visual culture of East Asia and explores the rise of modernities in parts of East Asia. It provides a thematically-grounded survey of issues, movements and artistic developments spanning the early modern and modern periods. Focus is paid to the role of cultural production in forging links within and across societies and more broadly, the relation of art with political, social, technological and economic change. Critical attention will also be given to the global interaction between Asia and the West, and its impact on ideological and theoretical frameworks that govern processes of image-making.

accessConditions.prerequisite: 12 credit points at 2000 level in Art History or 12 credit points at 2000 level in Asian Studies or (6 credit points at 2000 level in Art History and (CASF1001 and CASF1002))

learningOutcomes: achieve a better understanding of the modern art developments and its histories of all the countries discussed in the course
identify and interpret art works and practices produced in parts of Asia in the early modern and modern eras
critically evaluate the socio-political role of modern art in its historical context of formation
understand key theoretical models for interpreting modern East Asian art and its attendant issues
effectively and confidently articulate a sophisticated interpretation of this cultural production both verbally and in writing
expand your research experience and develop requisite research and analytical skills essential in the study of art history and visual culture.

units.name: On Photography and the Wretched Screen
units.description: This unit will draw on a wide range of photographic material, including university and museum collections, to examine the pivotal role of photography in recording and shaping our image-culture across diverse global contexts. The unit will engage with key debates to examine the social, cultural, theoretical, historical and art practice contexts of the photograph as an image and as an object. Key theories from Walter Benjamin to Hito Steyerl will be used to interrogate themes of memory, documentary and the real, witnessing, conflict, gender and sexuality, decolonisation, and the digital.

accessConditions.prerequisite: 12 credit points at 2000 level in Art History

learningOutcomes: develop advanced analytical and research skills to engage with the variety of photographic processes and technologies of production through encounters with key primary texts and photographs in local Sydney collections

gain a sophisticated understanding of the range of artistic, cultural and social functions, and significance of the photographic image from the advent of the medium in the 19th-century to our present moment

build practice, confidence and skill in oral and written presentation of material, both individually and as a group, and in analysing photographs in their multiple contexts of production and reception.

units.name: Gender and Sexuality in Asian Art History
units.description: This unit investigates issues of gender and sexuality in art, visual culture and art history in modern and contemporary Asia from the 19th century to the present. Students will explore women- and/or queer-centred histories of the production and reception of art, and the rise of feminist and queer art and art history in parts of Asia.

accessConditions.prerequisite: 12 credit points at 2000 level in Art History or (6 credit points at 2000 level in Art History and (CASF1001 and CASF1002))

learningOutcomes: achieve a better understanding of the impact and effect of sexual difference in the reading and writing of the art histories discussed in the course
identify and engage with issues of gender particular to a variety of art historical sub-fields
understand and articulate the stakes of gender within the larger ethics of the arts world
understand key feminist theories and feminist art historical discourses and its uses in the context for interpreting modern and contemporary Asian art and its attendant issues
engage with and apply larger questions of gender to students’ own art historical practices
expand research experience and develop requisite research and analytical skills essential in the study of art history and visual culture.
acquire and expand knowledge on Asian artists and cultural practitioners across a range of thematic issues relevant to gender

units.name: Art and the Aesthetics of the Everyday
units.description: Students study contemporary and historical art made in response to the ebb and flow of daily life and the material conditions of the street, the city, and the home. They study key texts of the art and politics of the everyday and topics related to the nineteenth, twentieth and twenty-first century theory and practice. Students will focus on artists who heighten awareness of the banal and mundane, of the detritus of life, of gendered distinctions between home and city, and the paradoxical revelation of the marvelous in the everyday.

accessConditions.prerequisite: 12 credit points at 2000 level in Art History or 6 credit points at 2000 level in Art History and CASF1001 and CASF1002

learningOutcomes: demonstrate a sound historical overview of the relevance of the everyday as a cultural and aesthetic concept
demonstrate acquisition of analytical tools and appropriate vocabulary needed to discuss historical and contemporary art
apply the acquisition of research skills in relation to the term 'the everyday'
ability to plan, structure and complete well-argued writing
demonstrate skill with visual analysis of objects and artworks
Communicate ideas effectively in academic discourse
Share ideas with peers in class

units.name: Objects and Problems at Chau Chak Wing Museum
units.description: This unit brings students into sustained contact with objects in the Chau Chak Wing Museum and challenges students to research and curate them. It is designed to build and test the key skills of art historians in the world - from basic analysis of materials and techniques to complex questions of cultural meaning - by analyzing objects and the challenges they pose.

accessConditions.prerequisite: 12 credit points at 2000 level in the Art History major

learningOutcomes: Demonstrate familiarity with a range of museum objects in different mediums and from different time periods
Identify and analyse materiality of objects and develop skills in critiquing cultural meanings
Understand the technical and social issues associated with objects from a historiographic perspective
Build and test key analytical skills required to discuss museum objects

units.name: Text, Image, Sound: Islamic Book Arts
units.description: This unit provides a thematic study of historical and contemporary book arts in the Islamic world, drawing on the art of painting and calligraphy as well as key texts to engage with the foundational interrelations between text, image, orality and other forms of sensory experience. Starting with early Qurans, we move to pre-modern illustrated manuscripts, and modern and contemporary works of art inspired by manuscript cultures, exploring histories of authorship, portraiture, patronage, workshop practices, audience and perception, as well as the collecting and display of manuscripts in museums. Several site visits to Sydneys various collections offer opportunities for object-based learning.

accessConditions.prerequisite: 12 credit points at 2000 level in Art History or 6 credit points at 2000 level in Art History and CASF1001 and CASF1002

learningOutcomes: By the end of this unit the student will be able to identify and analyse manuscripts and other works-on-paper from Islamic world.

By the end of this unit the student will be able to identify the common relationships between contemporary, modern and pre-modern works of art from the Islamic world and parse out historical inspirations in contemporary works of art.
By the end of this unit the student will be able to apply skills of observation and analysis of visual materials, extending and amplifying their critical practice.
By the end of this unit the student will be able to exhibit skills and abilities in presenting visual material through critical argument in extended written and oral presentations.
By the end of this unit the student will be able to assume responsibility for their own research methods and encounter the full spectrum of methods of research and scholarship.
By the end of this unit the student will be able to engage with peers during the preparation of tutorials, group discussions and oral presentations.

By the end of this unit the student will have encountered and engaged with a variety of traditions of book-making and will have explored the critical debates that relate these different traditions to broader, global histories of the book.

units.name: First Nations Art
units.description: This unit explores the range and depth of First Nations Art globally with special attention to the Indigenous Art and visual culture of Australia and North America. It is designed to explore not only the material and formal features of First Nations' art but the social, cultural and spiritual traditions in which it is embedded and the understandings of time, space and country that inform First Nations art. It also explores the debates that have surrounded the notion and definition of "First Nations" art in recent years.

accessConditions.prerequisite: 12 credit points at 2000 level in Art History, or (6 credit points at 2000 level in Art History and CASF1001 and CASF1002)

learningOutcomes: Demonstrate critical knowledge of First Nations art and its global traditions.
Demonstrate appropriate skills of critical analysis and persuasive writing and speaking on works of First Nations art
Encounter art ‘in situ’ in sustained and regular ways, interacting with objects and sites of study directly through fieldwork, museum-based learning and exhibition experience.
Engage with confidence in current critical debates and discussions in the field of First Nations art and encounter a range of methods of art historical enquiry.

units.name: A Material World: Cultures of Design
units.description: Design shapes how we live in the world. From dressing our bodies, to inhabiting carefully composed interiors, and encountering innovative objects, the limits of our understanding are frequently materially determined. In this unit, students will engage with design histories - both past and present - to understand how design forms our experience of the world. Close studies will be made of key objects, designers, and materials, building a fluency with design from a variety of cultures and movements. The unit will be delivered through object-based learning, providing students with an opportunity to connect with professional and real-world contexts as they explore design cultures.

accessConditions.prerequisite: 12 credit points at 2000 level in Art History

learningOutcomes: Demonstrate a critical command of the core body of knowledge concerning material culture and design studies
Analyse and reflect critically upon relevant scholarship and communicate this to others.
Undertake a close critical reading of a variety of design objects in alignment with current sector practices.
Effectively communicate research-based thinking in written work or oral presentations, for different audiences.

Demonstrate independence and initiative; integrity and maturity; the capacity to evaluate the work of others, including peers; and a considerable degree of autonomy to manage group and individual projects.

units.name: Fieldwork: Art and the City
units.description: This unit takes students out of the classrooms and into major world cities to explore not only the history of architecture and public space but also the galleries, collections and artworks housed in the city. It offers a vital opportunity for students to learn with and from artworks, buildings, spaces and monuments in situ. Fieldwork may take place in Summer or Winter Intensive periods.

accessConditions.prerequisite: 12 credit points at 2000 level in Art History or 6 credit points at 2000 level in Art History and CASF1001 and CASF1002

learningOutcomes: Students know in depth the fabric and artworks of a major city
Students confident in interpreting and analyzing works of art in situ, museum spaces, and architectural and sculptural formations of the city
Students give fluent and persuasive group presentations ‘on site’ and in front of objects
Students understand the deep importance of historical and geographical setting, and material composition, for the understanding of all works of visual art.
Students work together and individually to reflect on their experience and learning

units.name: Art, Cities and Early Modern Worlds
units.description: From Renaissance Italy to Safavid Persia and beyond, this course will take students across the globe to explore art in the cities and spaces of the Early Modern World. Works of art and design shaped and enriched the lives of these places. The course will take an expanded view of the distinct and interwoven visual and material histories of these worlds, exposing students to cutting-edge thinking, writing and exhibitions. You will encounter comparative, globally aware and materially expansive approaches to art through seminars, site visits and discussions led by a team of teachers dedicated to opening access to an expanded vista of these great cities, sites and works of art

accessConditions.prerequisite: 12 credit points at 2000 level in the Art History, or (6 credit points at 2000 level in Art History and CASF1001 and CASF1002)

learningOutcomes: Deepen your knowledge of art and architectural history, particularly of art , space and architecture in the Global Early Modern World
Amplify and develop critical skills in comparison and analysis of visual material especially across places, cultures and time periods.
Engage with new and pertinent methods in art history, from Digital Humanities methodologies to site-based research
Gain opportunity to use digital humanities tools and methods first-hand.

units.name: Sensation: Encountering Contemporary Art
units.description: Today transformations in how art is made, networked, theorised and curated is indelibly tied to new and expanded ways of encountering contemporary art. From political imperatives of decolonisation, globalisation and the environment, indigeneity, to feminist and queer art, or art as spectacle, new impetuses for artmaking and curating are dynamically changing the cultural landscape. Social media and the digital turn offer new modes of engaging with contemporary visual culture. This unit addresses these recent transformations to explore the expanded field of contemporary art in the digital sphere and in the physical encounter with art in local art spaces, galleries, biennales and beyond.

accessConditions.prerequisite: 12 credit points at 2000 level in Art History or (6 credit points at 2000 level in Art History and CASF1001 and CASF1002)

learningOutcomes: Understand and articulate key issues in contemporary art through critical analysis of objects, media, texts, and exhibition practice
Demonstrate appropriate skills of critical analysis and persuasive writing and speaking on works of contemporary art
Encounter art ‘in situ’ in sustained ways, interacting with objects and sites of study directly through fieldwork, gallery-based learning and exhibition experience.
Engage with confidence in current critical debates and discussions in the field of Contemporary art and encounter a range of methods of art historical enquiry.

units.name: Art History Honours Thesis 1
units.description: This unit involves research towards and preliminary writing of an Honours thesis of 18 000-20 000 words, in collaboration with a supervisor approved by the Art History Honours Coordinator.
learningOutcomes: As per graduate qualities

units.name: Art History Honours Thesis 2
units.description: In this unit you complete and submit your substantial, independent research project in Art History. Regular meetings with a supervisor approved by the Art History Honours Coordinator will guide your progress. You will continue to submit drafts at agreed times, and develop your expertise in relevant research methods and analytical skills as well as in the subject matter of your specialist topic.
learningOutcomes: As per graduate qualities

units.name: Art Is the Issue: Histories and Theories
units.description: This unit concentrates on key developments in the history of art history as a discipline. The seminar centres on selected polemical texts and disputes in the discipline, to demonstrate that much of what all art historians do is contested and problematic. From the question of what we should study to the always vexed question of 'how' we should study it, the aim of this unit is to give you a sense of both the history and the problematic of the discipline in which you will be engaged whether you intend careers as scholars, researchers, curators, or art writers.
learningOutcomes: obtain a grasp of the main lines of art-historical thinking in the last 200 years
develop and refine the ability to read critically in the literature of the discipline
appreciate the diverse ways works of art have been considered in differing historical contexts
undertake a sustained piece of writing and research in the essay of 6000 words.

units.name: The Past and Futures of Digital Cultures
units.description: This unit introduces Digital Cultures, the critical interdisciplinary field of research into the cultural and social dimensions of digital technologies. It explores the histories, imaginaries, ideas, platforms and thinkers that inform the study of digital cultures. Students will examine tools and theories that explain the interrelated processes of digital media and communications development and social change. This unit will explore what it means to be a digital cultures researcher and practitioner, offering students foundational knowledge and skills for the major as well as investigating the latest technologies and trends.
learningOutcomes: Understand the key concepts in the field of digital cultures, and have the ability to explain them and their interconnections across disciplinary perspectives.
Locate histories and imaginaries of digital cultures in fiction, scholarly works, and media platforms/ecosystems.
Identify the key thinkers that contributed to the development of the field, and explain their influence on the studies and practice of digital cultures.
Develop and demonstrate understanding of critical research process and be able to articulate it in academic writing.
Develop skills in visual design, critical thinking, and independent and collaborative research to create and present work in a range of formats and apply theories to issues in digital cultures.

units.name: Elements of Digital Cultures
units.description: This unit offers a comprehensive introduction to the core elements of digital cultures. Students will gain a combination of practical skills and theoretical understanding of digital elements including video, text, images, data, sound, algorithms and networks. Combining creative exercises with critical discussion, the unit will equip students with skills and concepts to plan, construct and deconstruct digital artefacts, in order to understand their significance within the digital cultures and communication fields.

accessConditions.assumedKnowledge: Familiarity with computers, smartphones and the internet

learningOutcomes: Analyse and explain key elements of digital cultures within their broader contexts.
Identify and articulate interconnections among various aspects of digital cultures.
Demonstrate foundational skills in utilizing digital tools effectively.
Critically evaluate and assess digital cultural objects, texts, and practices.
Create critically informed projects that integrate elements of digital cultures.

units.name: Internet Transformations
units.description: The Internet is a communications and media infrastructure that supports constant economic and social change, as well as being integrated into the routines of our everyday life across the planet. Internet Transformations critically examines the online technologies, platforms and industries at the heart of these changes. It introduces key skills in analysis, evaluation and critique of these objects, situated in a historical context. It also interrogates the implications of emerging internetworked phenomena such as the internet of things, augmented reality and algorithmic cultures.

accessConditions.prerequisite: (6 credit points at 1000 level in ARIN) or (12 credit points at 1000 level in MECO or SIEN or DECO) or (12 credit points in WRIT1001 and (ATHK1001 or ATHK1901))

learningOutcomes: demonstrate an understanding of the history, politics, economics and cultures of the internet and networked technologies
demonstrate skills in, and professional orientation to, web, social media and mobile media production
understand the affordances and limitations of online media and communications production software
discuss social and cultural issues arising from networked change
analyse and critique emerging internet phenomena eg. mixed reality, internet of things, smart cities.

units.name: Everyday Digital Media
units.description: How we eat, sleep, talk, love, shop, work, play, learn and die are all shaped by digital media. Everyday digital media focuses on the transformation of self and society through the digital mediation of everyday practices. How do we organise our social lives and engage creatively in online realms? What are the opportunities and risks of sharing and self-presentation in networked publics? How are communities reconfigured in a digital context? This unit introduces theories of digital culture and identity and applies them to our everyday experiences and interactions with social media, participatory culture, locative media, computer games, virtual reality, smart homes and connected cities.

accessConditions.prerequisite: 12 credit points at 1000 level in ARIN or MECO or SIEN or DECO or DESN or 12 credit points in WRIT1001 and (ATHK1001 or ATHK1901)

learningOutcomes: explain and analyse the role of everyday digital practices, interactions and routines in the transformation of self and society.
translate personal experiences and larger social issues into a scholarly form relevant for social research.
critically evaluate the efficacy of different arguments and perspectives in relation to contemporary debates about digital media, identity and social relations.
demonstrate the ability to understand key concepts and use them creatively and independently to understand larger contextual problems.
apply independent learning and collaborative research skills towards the crafting of well-supported and insightful arguments about digital media and society.

units.name: Technology and Culture
units.description: Technology and Culture explores the relationships between technological developments and cultural change, with a particular focus on digital media. This unit of study interrogates the changing theorisations of technology in society by tracing the influence of key texts in media studies, philosophy of technology, sociology, cultural studies and science and technology studies. Through close readings of advanced texts, students explore the significance of technology in social power, identity, gender, social shaping, class, space, assemblages, actor-networks, experience, thought, time, and materiality. We mobilise and evaluate these theories in relation to emerging technologies today.

accessConditions.prerequisite: (6 credit points at 2000 level in ARIN and (12 credit points at 1000 level in ARIN or 1000 level in MECO)) or (12 credit points at 2000 level in DECO) or (6 credit points at 1000 level and 6 credit points at 2000 level in SIEN or INFS)

learningOutcomes: Understand the complex interrelationship between technology and culture
Develop independent learning and critical thinking through readings, discussion and written assignments
Demonstrate oral and written communication skills by facilitating and participating in ‘provocations’
Research and inquiry skills, involving the ability to present evidence and argument in support of your own particular perspective
Become aware of the importance of influence and the conventions of citation, and a capacity to trace influences in this assignment
Apply theoretical approaches to the study of technology and culture to recent case studies
Use communication and information technologies effectively.

units.name: Social Media Cultural Production
units.description: This unit explores the rapidly evolving contexts and processes of digital cultural production and consumption. Drawing on a grounded knowledge of social media, digital influencers and platform cultures, students will critically evaluate issues relating to diversity, inclusion and social harms in contemporary social media ecologies. Students will analyse the technical, social and economic structures shaping digital cultural production and evaluate their own agency and opportunities for change-making. They will apply their skills in social media practice and demonstrate their emerging expertise in the field of digital cultures to produce social media artefacts and campaigns.

accessConditions.prerequisite: 6 credit points at 2000 level in ARIN and (12 credit points at 1000 level in ARIN or 1000 level in MECO)

learningOutcomes: identify and analyse the types, forms, features and functions of social media platforms.
demonstrate a critical understanding of the industrial, social and cultural context of social media production.
research, write, and produce social media artefact.
discuss the significance of professional issues such as platform regulation, content moderation, algorithmic visibility, and cultural representation to social media practice.

units.name: Researching Digital Cultures
units.description: How do people make and use new media technologies? To answer this question you need to know how to conduct research: a systematic investigation using carefully chosen and ethically sound methods. In this unit students prepare a research proposal to improve knowledge about the social implications of the latest developments in information technologies. They build their methodology by choosing a combination of methods: big data analysis; ethnography, interviews, surveys, online methods, discourse analysis, content analysis and/or case studies.

accessConditions.prerequisite: (6 credit points at 2000 level in ARIN and (12 credit points at 1000 level in ARIN or 1000 level in MECO)) or (12 credit points at 2000 level in DECO or DESN)

learningOutcomes: Identify and frame a research problem in digital cultures, articulating its significance and the methodological approaches appropriate to investigating it.
Critically survey existing scholarship in a defined area of digital media and society research, evaluating the methodological choices of existing studies and identifying gaps in current knowledge.
Apply and evaluate a range of digital research methods through structured practical exercises.

Design a methodologically coherent research proposal that demonstrates understanding of relevant theoretical frameworks, research methods, and ethical considerations appropriate to the study of digital cultures.
Collaborate effectively in a research team, negotiating a shared intellectual project, dividing and integrating work, and documenting individual contributions.
Communicate research problems and designs clearly and persuasively across different formats, including written and multimodal forms.

units.name: Digital Arts
units.description: Digital Arts explores the ways digital and new media technologies are being used to transform cultural production, distribution and reception in the visual and performing arts, machine vision and popular culture. Students will learn about the changing aesthetic, cultural and technical dimensions of new digital technologies and will develop the critical and analytical tools and a practical skillset with which to discuss, evaluate, and appreciate works of digital art.

accessConditions.prerequisite: 12 credit points at 2000 level in units with an ARIN or ARHT or FILM or DECO prefix or (6 credit points at 1000 level and 6 credit points at 2000 level in units of study with SIEN prefix)

learningOutcomes: demonstrate an understanding of the way digital technologies are used in a broad range of contemporary art practices including visual arts, performance, sound, machine vision, and interactive media

foster an appreciation of the cultural and aesthetic diversity of art practices utilising digital technologies, and understand the ways in which power relationships are challenged/contested/unsettled through art
develop a grounding in the contemporary theoretical debates, conceptual issues, and policy informing digital art practice
practice the ability to critically analyse and discuss a range of digital art works in written and oral forms and in a variety of genres
hone research and inquiry skills, involving the ability to present evidence to support an argument reflecting your own perspective

units.name: Games and Play
units.description: Games are distinctive cultural forms, with histories, aesthetics, design cultures, player communities and academic theory. This unit explores how games work, how they are situated in culture, and some of the practices behind designing and critically assessing games as media items. Drawing on game studies, game design, and media studies, students analyse games and develop a game concept from scratch.

accessConditions.prerequisite: (6 credit points at 2000 level in ARIN and (12 credit points at 1000 level in ARIN or 1000 level in MECO)) or (12 credit points at 2000 level in DECO) or (6 credit points at 1000 level and 6 credit points at 2000 level in SIEN)
accessConditions.assumedKnowledge: No prior programming experience necessary

learningOutcomes: understand the cultural relevance of computer games
critically examine the ethics, politics and everyday uses of mobile media and computer games
understand the persuasive and educative potential of computer games
generate feasible concepts for games
understand the way market dynamics, political economies and ideologies shape computer games
understand the ways in which computer games generate and facilitate specific cultural practices and identities.

units.name: Introduction to Asian Cultures
units.description: This unit introduces cultures of Asia across time, from the Ramayana to K-Pop. The curriculum aims to provide essential knowledge and skills necessary for more detailed study of Asia, including through laying the groundwork for comparative investigation of trans-Asian phenomena. Topics and themes include: religion, ritual, and philosophy; sacred kings and capitals; hierarchy and social order; family, kinship and gender systems; high art, literature and popular culture. This unit will demonstrate how deep cultural trends relate to contemporary Asian cultures.
learningOutcomes: Demonstrate awareness of key elements relevant to the study of Asian culture.
Describe—both orally and in writing—the key traits of Asia’s major cultural developments.
Apply the concept of a 'trans-national' approach to different Asian societies.
Challenge dominant narratives about Asia, demonstrating an awareness of complexity and change over time.

units.name: Asia: Past, Present, Future
units.description: This unit looks at Asia's past, present and future in a global perspective. It makes use of the new approaches of world history and big history, and moves along large spatial and temporal scales. This unit prepares students to make sense of specific Asia-related subjects offered in more advanced units of study. In doing so, we will also examine some of the challenges Asia is facing today and think about Asia's place in our increasingly globalised world.
learningOutcomes: explain how thresholds of increasing complexity, differing scales of time and space, and collective learning help us understand past, present, and future events in Asia as part of a larger narrative
integrate perspectives from multiple disciplines to evaluate the history of Asia as part of the history of the Earth and the Universe
define major features which shaped past and present Asia
describe the changing characteristics of Asian societies
analyse accelerating global change as reflected in Asia
identify important human and environmental issues that may affect the future of Asia
propose a vision of the future of Asia based on new understandings of the past
use key historical and scientific concepts and facts in constructing explanations
evaluate, analyse, and synthesise primary and secondary sources to form well-crafted written and oral arguments.

units.name: Korean Popular Culture
units.description: This unit presents multiple aspects of popular culture in South and North Korea, from K-pop to blockbuster movies, popular literature, internet culture, video games and socialist mass culture. It approaches Korea's cultural industries historically and critically, questioning their relationships to colonialism, militarism, social hierarchies, national identities, and economic globalization. Primary reading materials are drawn from a variety of genres and media to reflect the diversity of popular culture in the two Koreas. All reading materials are available in English translation and no knowledge of Korean is required.

accessConditions.prerequisite: 12 credit points from Korean Studies or 12 credit points at 1000 level from Asian Studies

learningOutcomes: Gain in-depth knowledge of how Korean popular culture is produced, distributed and consumed globally
Reflect about the specificities of Korean culture and its relationships to other cultures around the world
Develop critical thinking skills to be able to assess the economic, social and political aspects of contemporary cultural industries
Learn about concepts from the fields of art sociology, economics of culture, cultural studies and critical theory and apply them to the study of works of popular culture
Conduct research, weigh evidence and work critically with primary and secondary sources
Structure an academic essay and write clearly and concisely to make persuasive arguments
Develop oral presentation skills and learn to communicate ideas effectively

units.name: Buddhist Thought and Culture
units.description: This unit provides a survey of the major issues and core ideas of Buddhism from its beginnings to subsequent developments in others parts of Asia. Students will be introduced to Buddhist understanding of liberation, existence, and knowledge, with a focus on exploring how Buddhist thought and practices, such as ritual and meditation, shape each other in larger socio-cultural contexts.

accessConditions.prerequisite: 12 credit points at 1000 level from any combination of Ancient Greek or Ancient History or Anthropology or Arabic Language and Cultures or Archaeology or Art History or Asian Studies or Chinese Studies or Cultural Studies or Education or European Studies or French and Francophone Studies or Gender Studies or Germanic Studies or Hebrew or History or Indonesian Studies or International and Comparative Literary Studies or Italian Studies or Japanese Studies or Jewish Civilisation, Thought and Culture or Korean Studies or Latin or Linguistics or Philosophy or Psychology or Sanskrit or Sociology or Spanish and Latin American Studies or Visual Arts or 12 credit points at 1000 level from Studies in Religion

learningOutcomes: - demonstrate foundational understanding of the development of Buddhism as a religion shaped by historical and cultural forces
- articulate the relationship and interaction between Buddhist thought and the different expressions of the religion
- demonstrate understanding of the historically and culturally bound contexts within which Buddhism developed in different regions
- analyse issues underlying Buddhist thought and culture, and their impact on contemporary life
- Analyse presuppositions that shape the self-understanding of Buddhist traditions and their developments in Asia

units.name: Chinese Thought
units.description: This unit offers students the opportunity to explore China's major traditions of philosophy and practice through English translations of key texts as well as authoritative secondary studies. The main foci of the unit include the following major areas: diversity and polemics in early Chinese thought, developments in Daoism, Buddhist thought and influence, and Neo-Confucian (Daoxue) thought.

accessConditions.prerequisite: 12 credit points at 1000 level from Asian Studies or Chinese or Indonesian or Japanese or Korean Studies or Sanskrit or Philosophy or Studies in Religion

learningOutcomes: have a balanced and structured understanding of key developments in the history of Chinese philosophy.
identify, define and interpret a large number of theoretical positions which characterized the development of Chinese thought over the centuries.
approach key topics in an objective and coherent manner.
develop a capacity for critical thinking.
clearly express your ideas in correct English in both written and oral assessments.

units.name: Remaking Chinese Society, 1949-Present
units.description: The history of the People's Republic of China comprises two periods. In the Maoist era (1949-1978), the Communist-led government attempted to build a centrally planned, socialist society in which politics dominated people's daily lives. In the post-Mao era (since 1978), by contrast, the socialist institutions have largely been dismantled in pursuit of a market-based alternative. This unit of study explores key social, political, cultural and economic features of both periods and analyses the problems and paradoxes of transition.

accessConditions.prerequisite: 12 credit points at 1000 level from Asian Studies or Japanese Studies or Korean Studies or Chinese Studies or Indonesian Studies or Sanskrit or History or Ancient History
accessConditions.assumedKnowledge: Students with no prior knowledge of modern Chinese history are encouraged to read an introductory textbook (e.g., Edwin E. Moise. Modern China: A History. Second edition. Longman, 1994) before the start of the semester

learningOutcomes: have a better understanding of the origins and historical developments of the People's Republic of China (PRC)
have a better understanding of key social, ideological, political, geopolitical and economic factors which have informed the history of the PRC
approach key issues in an objective and structured manner
develop a capacity for critical thinking
clearly express your ideas in correct English in both written and oral assignments

units.name: Religious Traditions of South Asia
units.description: This unit introduces themes in South Asian religions from the Indus Valley Civilisation onward. Attention is paid to the social and cultural contexts in which Hinduism, Buddhism and Jainism emerged. Goddess traditions are discussed, as are concepts such as tantra, yoga and meditation, karma and rebirth and dharma. Texts such as Bhagavat Gita are also introduced. A focus will be on the implications of Classical India for an understanding of contemporary Asian cultures, particularly those of South and Southeast Asia.

accessConditions.prerequisite: 12 junior credit points from Table A

learningOutcomes: be able to place South Asian religious, literary, philosophical, contemplative, social and artistic expression into larger contexts of historical and doctrinal developments
be able to place social and political movements into larger religious and intellectual contexts of South Asian culture
have an appreciation of the ways in which self-understanding develops through the interaction between its artistic, religious and literary traditions
be aware of the significance of South Asian religions in understanding the emergence and development of religious structures across Asia as a whole
have a methodological awareness of issues in cross-cultural research in the humanities
have acquired a solid foundation for further studies of South Asia, Buddhism and Asian Studies in general

units.name: Tantric Buddhism in India and Tibet
units.description: Buddhism is a trans-Asian phenomenon originating in India. The doctrines and practices of late Indian and tantric Buddhism contain manifold philosophies, deities and rituals. They spread to Tibet from the 8th Century onward and interacted with and influenced Chinese and Mongolian cultures. This unit provides an overview of the philosophical systems and practices of Mahayana and tantric Buddhism which emerged in India and were re-imagined in Tibet. It also explores how pre-modern cultural interactions with Indian and Chinese traditions provided ideological contexts for the Tibetan religious and political institutions.

accessConditions.prerequisite: 12 credit points at 1000 level in Asian Studies or Japanese Studies or Korean Studies or Chinese Studies or Indonesian Studies or Sanskrit or History or Studies in Religion

learningOutcomes: place religious, social and political movements within larger historical and ideological contexts
place contemporary issues in interactions between India, China and Tibet within larger historical and ideological contexts
demonstrate methodological awareness of issues in cross-cultural research in the humanities

appreciate the ways in which a culture’s understanding of itself develops through the interaction between its social, cultural and religious traditions, and how these are expressed in the emergence of its political institutions
appreciate the ways in which cultural self-understanding is constantly shaped and reshaped through interactions with other cultures
demonstrate a solid foundation for further studies of India, China and Tibet, and Asian Studies in general
demonstrate analytical skills that will enrich their studies in fields beyond Asian Studies.

units.name: Buddhism, Meditation, and Brain
units.description: This unit of study introduces students to Buddhist meditation practices, tracing their evolution from the time of the Buddha to the techniques of Tibetan tantra. It explores how these practices intersect with modern cognitive science to improve our understanding of human cognition, including attention, memory, and perception. It critically addresses the popularisation of meditation in the West, clarifying the distinctions between meditation and mindfulness, and discusses meditation's historical significance and diverse forms within Buddhism. Students will explore foundational interdisciplinary concepts, enhancing their appreciation of meditation's role across different cultures and times.

accessConditions.prerequisite: 12 credit points at 1000 level in Asian Studies

learningOutcomes: Describe the historical evolution of Buddhist meditation across various traditions, demonstrating an understanding of Asia's major religious and cultural movements.
Provide alternative perspectives on contemporary understandings of meditation in Asia.
Critically analyse the popularity of meditation in Western contexts, distinguishing between different forms of meditation and their purposes.
Understand how cognitive science theories explain aspects of meditation, such as its effects on attention, memory, and perception
Develop a capacity to engage in interdisciplinary Asian studies, synthesising information from religious studies, psychology, and neuroscience
Work collaboratively in cross-cultural and interdisciplinary settings, applying basic knowledge of meditation practices to enhance dialogue and understanding between diverse cultural perspectives.

units.name: Samurai and Merchants: Tokugawa Japan
units.description: Tokugawa Japan (1603-1868) had a complex feudal structure articulated around the shogun, the feudal lords and their samurai retainers. It also had huge cities, birthplaces of some of the first modern ways of life. The tensions between the feudal framework and the embryonic modernity of Tokugawa society make a fascinating case study in the non-Western world of what is to be modern. To do so, we shall follow a cross disciplinary approach: history, politics, sociology, economy, religion, arts and literature.

accessConditions.prerequisite: 12 credit points at 1000 level each in either Asian Studies or History

learningOutcomes: demonstrate understanding of the general trends of history of Japan
apply analytical skills to the study of the social models present in pre modern Japan
develop cross cultural competences through comparison of different cultural systems

units.name: Modern Korea
units.description: This unit aims to introduce some of the major issues in the history of Korea in the late 19th century and the last century. Topics include contradictions of the late Choson dynasty society; opening of Korea to the West and Japan and the attendant wave of reforms and rebellions; Japan's colonial rule; Korea's fight for freedom; liberation and division of Korea in 1945 and the subsequent process of nation-building in the two Koreas.

accessConditions.prerequisite: 12 credit points at 1000 level

learningOutcomes: Acquire in-depth knowledge of modern Korean history and society.
Learn interdisciplinary approaches to Korean studies, combining history, politics, and sociology.
Conduct undergraduate level research and write academic essays.
Communicate effectively through discussions and by presenting on complex historical materials.
Think critically and analytically about different societies and historical pasts.

units.name: History of Modern Indonesia
units.description: This unit examines the history of Indonesia, the world's fourth most populous country, emphasizing the interaction between Islam, nationalism and democracy. The unit traces these forces impact on the formation of modern Indonesia from the late nineteenth century, highlighting the experience and legacy of colonialism, the independence struggle, and the rise and fall of military rule. Particular attention is given to changing notions of national identity, debates about the place of Islam in the polity and authoritarianism and democratisation.

accessConditions.prerequisite: 12 Junior credit points in units of study listed in Table A

learningOutcomes: Demonstrate understanding of the structures of Indonesian history
Demonstrate ability to evaluate primary and secondary sources
Show appreciation of different perspectives on Indonesia and different ways of seeing the past
Show ability to research, synthesise and analyse a range of sources in order to produce informed arguments
Evaluate digital sources in researching and communicating concepts in Indonesian history.
Apply ethical standards to inquiry in Indonesian history particularly relating to decolonisation.

units.name: Social Activism in Southeast Asia
units.description: This unit examines country-specific and transnational social movements in Southeast Asia, including those focused on labour, women, the environment, and identity. During the semester we will explore how these movements emerged, what they have sought to achieve and how successful they have been in promoting social change in the Southeast Asian region. The unit adopts a multidisciplinary approach based on contemporary case study material from Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand, the Philippines and Singapore.

accessConditions.prerequisite: 12 junior credit points from Table A

learningOutcomes: Critically discuss the nature and role of selected social movements in Southeast Asia, drawing on theoretical frameworks derived from social movement studies and political science
Present coherent and analytically rigorous academic arguments in oral and written form
Contribute effectively and collaboratively to in-class discussions and small group work
Develop a research project and conduct independent and critical analysis using a range of academic materials

units.name: Understanding Southeast Asia
units.description: This unit of study introduces Southeast Asia. It emphasises the importance of geographical, political, economic, social and cultural context to our understanding of complex real-world problems. Having gained insight into these aspects of contemporary Southeast Asia, students learn to apply an interdisciplinary approach to the analysis of challenges faced by the region such as economic and social inequality, environmental management, food security and urbanisation.

accessConditions.prerequisite: 12 Junior credit points

learningOutcomes: demonstrate familiarity with key aspects of the cultures, history, geography and the political and economic systems of Southeast Asia.
recognise how a range of disciplines may be used to analyse complex, real-world, problems in a Southeast Asian context.
apply interdisciplinary methods to analyse Southeast Asian issues.
demonstrate ability to synthesise a range of different forms of information.
present evidenced-based arguments on Southeast Asian topics in a persuasive manner.
construct arguments that demonstrate differences between academic and policy writing genres.

units.name: Southeast Asian Transnationalisms
units.description: This unit considers Southeast Asia as an interconnected region that has been shaped and reshaped by cross-border relationships. Taking a multidisciplinary approach, it examines topics including historical and religious connections, capital and labour, environmental disasters, medical tourism and popular culture. Students will analyse these various forms of transnationalism and their influence in different Southeast Asian societies. By focusing on these regional dynamics rather than country-specific contexts, they will develop an understanding of Southeast Asia as a region constituted not only as a series of nation-states but by ongoing processes of connection, mobility and exchange.

accessConditions.prerequisite: (12 credit points at 1000 level in Asian Studies or Sociology or Politics or International Relations) or (12 credit points at 1000 or 2000 or 3000 level in Indonesian Studies)

learningOutcomes: Demonstrate a nuanced understanding of Southeast Asia as a region
Independently access and evaluate primary and secondary sources that relate to Southeast Asian transnationalism
Critically analyse and formulate arguments about the impact of different transnationalisms in Southeast Asia
Engage with, and apply, different concepts and theoretical perspectives to Southeast Asian case studies
Identify, define, investigate, and think critically and independently about critical problems in contemporary Southeast Asia
Apply appropriate professional and ethical standards to academic research and inquiry in Asian Studies

units.name: Field Study of Southeast Asia
units.description: Students will travel to Southeast Asia to undertake supervised, in-country field study. Focusing on a complex, real-world issue (e.g. urbanisation, women's empowerment, disability and social inclusion), students will consider the issue from a multidisciplinary perspective, including geographical, political, economic, social and cultural. While in the destination country, students will work in small multidisciplinary groups to conduct a mini research project. *Note that this unit is subject to travel and health advice at the time the unit is offered and may be delivered virtually. For more information please contact the unit coordinator.

accessConditions.prerequisite: 24 credit points at 1000 level

learningOutcomes: Demonstrate familiarity with key aspects of the Southeast Asian region, including its cultures, history and geography and its political and economic systems
Demonstrate the ability to draw on insights provided by a range of disciplines when analysing complex real-world problems in a Southeast Asian context
Present evidence-based arguments in academic and policy genres
Work in interdisciplinary groups to understand and deconstruct complex social issues.

units.name: Japan in East Asia
units.description: This unit places the modern and contemporary history of Japan within its East Asian context. We will examine a number of key events and subjects pertaining to the relations between Japan, China and Korea. Doing so we will touch sensitive and controversial topics, become aware of differing views of history prevalent in these countries and understand why the historical question constitutes a major political issue in East Asia.

accessConditions.prerequisite: 12 credit points at 1000 level from ASNS or JPNS or KRNS or CHNS or INMS or INGS or SANS or HSTY

learningOutcomes: define the major events which shaped the relations between Japan, China and Korea from the mid-nineteenth century until today
compare key developments in the modern and contemporary history of Japan, China and Korea
state the major historical issues at stake in contemporary East Asia and discuss their differing interpretations

become aware - through the use of primary and secondary sources, points of view, and frames of reference - of the differing views of history prevalent today in Japan, Korea (ROK and DPRK), and China (PRC and Taiwan), as well as of the various interpretations of history existing inside some of these countries
analyse primary and secondary historical sources, synthesise information, identify an argument and evaluate it
consider the meaning of history, historical perspective, and historical objectivity
develop your generic skills of oral and written communication and critical thinking

units.name: Youth and Language in Asia
units.description: This advanced unit explores the relationship between young people, language and society in Asia, with a particular focus on Southeast Asia and East Asia. It equips students with theoretical knowledge and analytical tools for examining language and sociocultural practices among youth in a range of contexts and their relationship with practices in wider society. Materials focusing on language in different societies in Asia will enable students to reflect critically on the complex interconnection between young people and mobility, belonging and participation within (global) communities, nations and peer-groups.

accessConditions.prerequisite: 12 credit points at 2000 level in Asian Studies or 12 credit points at 2000 level in Indonesian Studies

learningOutcomes: demonstrate familiarity with key issues in the relationship between youth, language and society in Asia
demonstrate familiarity with theoretical concepts relevant for analysing youth language practices
demonstrate the ability to identify, evaluate and apply scholarly evidence to support argument in written and spoken presentations
demonstrate the ability to construct and defend sound arguments using evidence from Asian societies and cultures
demonstrate high-level communication skills in written and spoken English

units.name: Modern Japan
units.description: You will learn the story of the changing life of the Japanese people since the mid-19th century until today, from the momentous Meiji reforms to the emergence of new social forces in the twentieth century, from the devastation of the Second World War to the trauma of the Fukushima nuclear disaster.

accessConditions.prerequisite: 12 credit points at 2000 level in Asian Studies or History or Japanese Studies

learningOutcomes: explain the major social, political, economic, and cultural transformations that have shaped Japan from the mid-nineteenth century to the present, from a relatively isolated agrarian society to an industrialised imperial power before 1945, and subsequently to a post-industrial global economic power.
