The unit deals with topics such as: the statistical nature of financial data; the specification, estimation and testing of financial econometric models for the asset return distribution; and the analysis of intra-day high frequency financial data. Throughout the unit, students are encouraged, especially in assignments, to familiarise themselves with financial data and learn how to apply the models to these data.
learningOutcomes: Become familiar with the stylized facts of financial data and with the econometric methods for analyzing such data.
Understand the key features of the classic and state-of-art econometric models used in financial economics.
Implement the econometric models in statistical packages, apply them to the data, and interpret the output from these models.

units.name: Topics in Applied Business Forecasting
units.description: This unit aims to introduce (i) the time series econometrics required for making forecasting; and (ii) the practice of forecasting in business. Forecasting requires both practical experience in model building and some statistical theory. On theoretical and empirical grounds, forecasting examples in various fields are discussed. At the end of this unit, students should be able to understand the major techniques of forecasting and be able to forecast actual time series using a statistical program. Topics covered include: the aims of forecasting and relation to time series analysis; types of time series; time series modelling and forecasting techniques; practical examples of forecasting.
learningOutcomes: demonstrate understanding of important econometric methods and their applicability to forecasting
utilise regression techniques for forecasting, including ARIMA, GARCH, and VAR modelling
apply a range of models to the forecasting of economic data
evaluate forecast accuracy for different techniques.

units.name: Topics in International Trade
units.description: This unit covers recent advancements in the field of international trade from both theoretical and empirical angles. It covers neoclassical trade theory such as models of comparative advantage, specific factors model, and the Heckscher-Ohlin model. It then covers new trade theory, including models with heterogeneous products, with homogeneous and heterogeneous firms, and models of international production. The unit concludes with a discussion of trade policy, which includes the analysis of the effects of tariffs and trade quotas upon trade under various market structures; the formation and design of regional trade agreements and the strategic behaviour of multinational enterprises.
learningOutcomes: demonstrate skills in oral and written communication (through class discussions, tests and essay)
demonstrate skills in problem solving (through tutorial questions and tests)
demonstrate critical thinking (through class discussions, tests, tutorial questions and essay)
demonstrate basic modelling skills (through tutorial questions and tests)
identify and intuitively explain the key issues in international trade theory and policy
understand the importance of assumptions in the economic modelling of international trade
distinguish between the efficiency implications and distributional consequences of trade and trade policy
understand the role of politics in trade and vice versa
assess the costs and benefits of trade policy from an economic point of view
feel sufficiently informed to confidently participate in public policy discussions and be ready to challenge some of the misconceptions regarding trade and globalisation.

units.name: Topics in Structural Econometrics
units.description: In this unit students will learn a combination of theoretical economic tools and related statistical techniques to be able to build and estimate structural econometric models. Students will be exposed to and be required to apply standard inference and estimation tools used in structural econometric estimations. Students will apply these techniques to datasets to analyse canonical structural economic questions related to topics that may include firm production behaviour, consumer choices, and game theoretic predictions.
learningOutcomes: Become familiar with the idea of structural modeling and reduced form estimation.
Learn the firm behavioural modeling techniques and learn to estimate production function.
Learn the discrete choice model, demand side model, the BLP model; Understand the econometric modelling of game theory.
Understand basic computation methods using MATLAB; Learn to compute GMM estimator.
Familiar with tools in the structural econometric modelling, and be able to apply GMM estimation and maximal likelihood estimation to different econometric settings.

units.name: Special Topic in Economic Analysis 1
units.description: This unit of study facilitates access to economics units outside the Honours program, such as those offered at postgraduate level. As such, the topic and availability of the unit varies from semester to semester, and students should seek the approval of the Honours coordinator to enrol.
learningOutcomes: identify asymmetric information aspects of economic interactions
design the incentive constraints and formulate objectives under such constraints
master the appropriate techniques and approaches

units.name: Special Topic in Economic Analysis 2
units.description: This unit of study facilitates access to economics units outside the Honours program, such as those offered at postgraduate level. As such, the topic and availability of the unit varies from semester to semester, and students should seek the approval of the Honours coordinator to enrol.
learningOutcomes: understand the objective of statistical machine learning
understand different machine learning methods, including basic mathematical derivations
identify applications to which certain machine learning methods can be applied
evaluate advantages and disadvantages of different machine learning methods.

units.name: Topics in Analysis of Panel Data
units.description: Research in economics, finance, marketing and accounting has been enriched by increased availability of panel data. A 'panel' refers to the pooling of observations on a cross section of households, countries, firms or individuals over several time periods, offering major advantages over conventional cross-sectional or time series data sets. This unit teaches students a comprehensive set of tools for the analysis of panel data, enabling students to both critically assess and contribute to applied economic research.
learningOutcomes: understand the models and econometric methods extensively used in analysis of panel data
critically evaluate existing empirical studies of panel data from economics and other fields
implement empirical projects using panel data and clearly demonstrate the ideas.

units.name: Special Topic in Econometrics 1
units.description: This unit of study facilitates access to econometrics units outside the Honours program, such as those offered at postgraduate level. As such, the topic and availability of the unit varies from semester to semester, and students should seek the approval of the Honours coordinator to enrol.
learningOutcomes: Become familiar with the idea of structural modeling and reduced form estimation.
Learn the firm behavioral modeling techniques and learn to estimate production function.
Learn the discrete choice model, demand side model, the BLP model. Understand the econometric modeling of game theory.
Understand basic computation methods using MATLAB. Learn to compute GMM estimator.

units.name: Special Topic in Econometrics 2
units.description: This unit of study facilitates access to econometrics units outside the Honours program, such as those offered at postgraduate level. As such, the topic and availability of the unit varies from semester to semester, and students should seek the approval of the Honours coordinator to enrol.
learningOutcomes: Describe and summarise economic time series data using appropriate statistical tools;

Develop an appreciation for the most widely-used econometric methods for quantifying knowledge about the underlying structure of the macroeconomy, and understand the practical challenges in implementing these methods;
Use MATLAB proficiently for a range of macroeconometric analysis;
Critically evaluate applied macroeconometric research, and understand some of the problems and solutions that arise in applied work.

units.name: Economics as a Social Science
units.description: This unit explores different views about the economy, the role of government, policies, and the causes, social and political aspects of economic events. You are introduced to the principal schools of economic thought -Classical, Marxian, Institutional, Neoclassical, Keynesian and Contemporary Political Economy. You will learn to apply these different perspectives to a political economy analysis of contemporary issues like climate change, social protest, the gig economy, wage theft, and global health pandemics. You will study the analytical focus, core concepts and insights of the different schools of economic thought within the context of the historical development of capitalist economies.
learningOutcomes: Demonstrate literacy in basic economic concepts.
Analyze the strengths and limitations of basic analytical tools used in economic analysis.
Independently gather information from libraries and other sources.
Evaluate information collected to construct answers to economic questions.
Explain the connections between different views on economic issues and different schools of economic thought.
Demonstrate the capacity for thinking critically about contemporary political economic issues.
Create clearly written arguments about political economic issues.

units.name: Global Economy: Production-Trade-Finance
units.description: This unit explores global economic integration, especially the renewed 'globalisation' from the 1980s. You will be introduced to different explanatory theories of changing historical patterns. You will analyse debates about whether increased trade, production and financial integration has been for the better or worse, and who have been the winners and the losers. You will concurrently explore the forms of, and debates about, the regulation of economic activity on a global scale, addressing the development and changing roles of states and international agencies.
learningOutcomes: gather, organise and use information from a variety of sources
develop reasoned arguments underpinned by evidence, and critically evaluate underlying theories, concepts, assumptions and limitations
evaluate arguments in disciplinary and cross-disciplinary fields of study
understand a broad range of complex and changing social, political and economic contexts
demonstrate an openness to new ways of thinking and appreciate the importance of intellectual curiosity and reflection as the foundation for continuous learning.

units.name: Economic Theories of Capitalism
units.description: This unit is designed to extend your understanding of the workings of the evolving capitalist economy. You will do this by critically engaging with economic theory which will deepen your knowledge of different schools of economic thought introduced to you in ECOP1001. This critical engagement will enable you to evaluate the fundamental economic features of capitalism such as: the role of markets in social provisioning and capital accumulation; class and inequality; the workings of money and finance; the nexus between unemployment and inflation; the tension between economic growth and the environment; and innovation and technological change.

accessConditions.prerequisite: 12 credit points at 1000 level in Political Economy

learningOutcomes: understand the conceptual underpinnings of the relevant theories
understand their limitations and the reasons for disagreement within economics
understand the political and historical context of the theories
formulate and express well-grounded views about the workings of the capitalist economy and theories about it.

units.name: Social Foundations of Capitalism
units.description: This unit examines the ways in which the economic activities of capitalism are 'embedded' within a much broader social structure. To do this, you will study the nature, structure, and relations of capitalism’s core institutions such as capital, labour, households, and the state. You will consider the conflict, contradiction, and cohesion inherent in the relationships between these institutions with respect to the racialised, classed, gendered and environmental processes of capital accumulation.

accessConditions.prerequisite: (12 credit points at 1000-level in Political Economy) or (6 credit points at 1000-level in Political Economy and BPPE1000)

learningOutcomes: demonstrate analytical skills in appraising the role of social forces and institutions in the dynamics of capital accumulation
apply broad conceptual structures to contemporary social and political issues
critically evaluate underlying theories, concepts, assumptions, limitations and arguments in disciplinary and crossdisciplinary fields of study
appreciate new ways of thinking and the importance of intellectual curiosity and reflection as the foundation for continuous learning
demonstrate research skills in the retrieval of relevant information
demonstrate skills in written and oral communication
negotiate and create shared understandings by respectfully interacting with people from diverse backgrounds.

units.name: Economic Policy and the State
units.description: One of the most contentious issues in economic debates concerns the role of the state in responding to contemporary economic and social problems such as financial crises, ruptures in relations with major trading partners, or pandemics like COVID-19. In this unit, you will interrogate the contemporary economic policies of the Australian state. You will consider: how these macroeconomic policies have evolved as they have been shaped by different economic theories, interests, and ideologies; how these policies actually operate in practice; and, how a nation-state’s economic policies are influenced by international economic factors.

accessConditions.prerequisite: 12 credit points at 1000 level in Political Economy

learningOutcomes: critically analyse and competently discuss the underlying macroeconomic frameworks of the predominant policy stances since the Great Depression
understand how the history of economic and social events has influenced the development of the role of the state, economic thinking and policy design
demonstrate the ability to conduct independent research that builds on the class materials in an original way
recognise and evaluate the alternative political economic traditions and their policy recommendations
engage with peers regarding various issues in economic policy
learn sources of data as well as how to access them and present data.

units.name: Social and Economic Inequalities
units.description: Social and economic inequalities are rampant across all nations even as equality is legitimised as a political norm. In this unit, you will seek to understand this paradoxical situation. You will: be introduced to key theoretical questions about equality, meritocracy and distribution; investigate the historical development of inequality within and between countries; and, examine the economic and political mechanisms through which inequality is reproduced in modern societies. You will also consider possible alternatives to this paradox including policy responses.

accessConditions.prerequisite: 12 credit points at 1000 level in Political Economy

learningOutcomes: demonstrate knowledge of different theories of the distribution of income and wealth
demonstrate knowledge of patterns of economic inequality
apply theories and concepts to study specific issues
make links between economic and political questions
construct a sound argument based on evidence and communicate this effectively (both verbally and in writing)
critically examine received ideas and existing institutions.

units.name: Race, Gender and Class
units.description: This unit introduces you to some of the big debates in the social sciences, through an exploration of the meaning and limits of class concepts in social theory. You will consider structure and agency, theory and praxis, gender, race, and the contemporary relevance of class. Your knowledge will be extended as you explore the methods used for the empirical study of race, gender and class. You will learn to communicateideas verbally and in clear readable prose through an oral presentation and structured essays. This unit adds breadth to the range of political economy issues you have studied previously and adds depth to your political economy analytical and writing skills.

accessConditions.prerequisite: 12 credit points at 2000 level in Political Economy

learningOutcomes: Recognise and understand the concepts of class theory and its relationship with issues of race and gender.
Understand debates about the meaning and limits of class concepts in social theory.
Develop a sense of the ‘politics of theory,’ by attention to the context dependence of the language (and thus, the theoretical concepts) of social science.
Develop a capacity for careful, critical analysis of arguments and evidence in social science.
Communicate ideas via oral presentation and engage peers verbally in analytical discussions about class theories and their limitations.
Convey theoretical and empirical ideas in clear and readable prose, express these ideas succinctly, and demonstrate an argument through structured essays with examples.

units.name: Environmental Political Economy
units.description: This unit explores the relationship between our economy and environment. It compares different ways of understanding this relationship including environmental economics, ecological economics, Marxist ecology and eco-feminism. Students will learn how these schools diagnose environmental problems as products of market failures, limits to growth or social inequalities. Students will examine different policy solutions for creating more sustainable economies, such as market mechanisms, steady state economies and environmental justice. Students will apply debates on the political economy of the environment through case studies of issues such as climate change, biodiversity loss and water scarcity.

accessConditions.prerequisite: 12 credit points at 2000 level in Political Economy

learningOutcomes: understand theories of economy-environment relations
examine the nature and causes of environmental challenges
evaluate competing policy approaches
produce well-researched pieces of work.

units.name: Money and Finance
units.description: The capitalist economy is organised around the circulation and pursuit of money. The financial system is neither a parasite on nor a veil over the 'real economy'; it is the organiser and disciplinarian of capitalism as an economic system, and it also breaks down from time to time, sometimes spectacularly. In this unit, you will explore: the evolution of money from the gold standard to the present; and, the institutions, instruments, and markets of modern finance, with a special focus on financial innovation and its challenges. You will critically engage with mainstream and other economic theories of finance, and apply these to understanding real world financial structures and events.

accessConditions.prerequisite: 12 credit points at 2000 level in Political Economy

learningOutcomes: demonstrate an understanding of the evolution, trends and debates of the current financial system
interpret and evaluate evidence and arguments about trends in international money and finance
develop relevant arguments based on critical evaluation of available evidence and use these to argue positions
apply economic theories and concepts to contemporary policy problems and practice
critically evaluate underlying theories, concepts, assumptions, limitations and arguments in financial theory
appreciate the advancing nature of knowledge frontiers in financial theory and practice through research

units.name: Development and Environment in India
units.description: This is an intensive 3 week integrated program of classes and field visits on the political economy of development and environmental management in India. The course provides students with a cross-disciplinary international learning experience in which they develop familiarity with an important Asian regional economy and the cultural competency to do research in this context.

accessConditions.prerequisite: 12 credit points at 2000 level in Political Economy

learningOutcomes: explain the meaning and contextual usage of key terms used by human geographers and political economists in the analysis of development and environmental sustainability, specifically in the Indian context
use field observation as a method for analysing urban and natural landscapes
undertake academic literature searches and to be aware of the conventions relating to academic literature
undertake problem-solving research into developmental and environmental issues
appraise issues relating to contemporary debates about development and environment in India.

units.name: History of Australian Capitalism
units.description: This unit focuses on the rich political-economic historiography of Australian capitalism. You will explore a range of themes in this historiography which include: British colonisation and First Nation's dispossession; the long economic booms and depressions since the 18th century; the progressive and evolving integration of Australia with the global economy through trade, capital flows and migration; the making and remaking of class relations, and social protest; the evolving embeddedness of the Australian economy in the natural environment (including the growing reliance on extractive sectors like mining); and, the financialisation of the everyday life of Australians.

accessConditions.prerequisite: 12 credit points at 2000 level in Political Economy

learningOutcomes: have broad knowledge about the economic and social history of Australia
critically analyse and competently discuss important themes in the historiography of Australian capitalism
critically analyse the relationship between social science and historiography
develop written arguments involving social theory and historical evidence
communicate quantitative social history data effectively
use information technology and library resources to conduct historical research.

units.name: Economic Cycles and Instability
units.description: This unit journeys through episodes of crises and instability in order to understand their key dynamics are embedded within historical, institutional and social contexts. You will study why some crises have a cyclical character while others do not, and how crisis contains elements to unlock the secrets of present-day and future sources of instability. To detect patterns (trends, cycles and volatility), you will be trained to use basic time series techniques for data analysis which will also assist you to undertake a project that evaluates sources of instability and discusses the challenges for policymakers to soften the ill-effects of economic downturns and create conditions for recovery.

accessConditions.prerequisite: 12 credit points at 2000 level in Political Economy

learningOutcomes: demonstrate working knowledge of the history and theory of cyclical behaviour in capitalist economies
understand how cycles can influence various aspects of modern-day societies (e.g., unemployment and income distribution)
apply quantitative skills learned in this unit to detect cyclical patterns (e.g., indexes, moving averages and time series analysis)
demonstrate the ability to conduct independent research which builds on the class material in an original way
analyse thematic questions and current issues concerning the structure of economic policies to combat the onset and ill effects of cycles.

units.name: Global Capitalism: Uneven Development
units.description: This unit examines the development of the capitalist world economy. You will analyse the explanations offered by different theoretical perspectives of the long-term historical and uneven development which has occurred. To understand the dimensions, scale and implications of this uneven development of global capitalism, you will consider: capitalism’s origins and Great Transformation; the post-World War long boom; the international monetary system’s formation and crisis; the global role played by the United States; the development of growth poles in Europe and Asia; the Global Financial Crisis; the Arab Spring; drug war capitalism; and, the possibilities for non-capitalist development.

accessConditions.prerequisite: 12 credit points at 2000 level in Political Economy

learningOutcomes: Demonstrate critical analytical skills in appraising the role of economic and social forces, and institutions, in the dynamics of capital accumulation.
Critically evaluate the theories, concepts, assumptions, strengths and limitations, and debates about capitalist development in different disciplinary fields of study.
Show openness to new ways of thinking and appreciate the importance of intellectual curiosity and reflection as the foundation for continuous learning.
Demonstrate an ability to negotiate and create shared understandings by respectfully interacting with people from diverse backgrounds.

units.name: Work and Labour
units.description: This unit examines the changing character and organisation of work. You will explore how the global economic dynamics of production, trade, and finance, the regulation of migration, automation and robotics, and evolving digital platforms of work and its organisation, shape the everyday experience of work and everyone's wellbeing. You will investigate the relationships between the formal and informal sectors of contemporary capitalist economies, and waged and non-waged labour, as well as the ways in which key institutions - including the state, capital, unions, and households - shape patterns of work and capital accumulation.

accessConditions.prerequisite: 12 credit points at 2000 level in Political Economy

learningOutcomes: Differentiate concepts of work, labour and employment
Articulate and evaluate different theories of work and labour
Describe and analyse changes in the organisation of capitalist work over time
Apply theories of capitalist work and labour to different contexts
Communicate, in both verbal and written form, a persuasive analysis of work and labour dynamics

units.name: Global Development
units.description: This unit is about the political economy of global development. Students are introduced to contemporary debates about the meaning and measurement of poverty and development in emerging economies, how development theory shapes economic history, and current policy trends. Students will learn to evaluate the socio-economic dynamics and impact of development policy, including new models of development finance and aid, the use of social policy as a development tool and the critical role that gender, climate change and labour migration play in the development experience.

accessConditions.prerequisite: 12 credit points at 2000 level in Political Economy

learningOutcomes: understand key theoretical and conceptual debates in the political economy of development in emerging economies
think critically about major themes in the political economy of contemporary development
assemble data relevant to economic development questions and analyse the relevant debates
write a critical, well-researched, original, and well-argued essay or report in an area of significance to emerging economies and the contemporary economic development debate
interact creatively and respectfully, in person and through online tools, with colleagues around key debates in the political economy of development and wellbeing.

units.name: Gender, Work, and Care in Economic Life
units.description: This unit examines gender in the global context. Gender is an important social relation that shapes the political economies of developed and developing countries. The unit focuses on gender relations as a subject of economic thought and analysis. It explores the ways in which contemporary gendered patterns of employment, production, distribution and exchange have been shaped historically and institutionally.

accessConditions.prerequisite: 12 credit points at 2000 level in Political Economy

learningOutcomes: Demonstrate a sophisticated understanding of gender as a multi-dimensional social structure that shapes everyday practices as well as the organisation of states and economies
Understand and assemble gender disaggregated data relevant to questions of gender (in)equality and change
Demonstrate an understanding of the conceptual and political differences between different political economy theories and articulate your position clearly
Demonstrate a critical understanding of key gender-related political economy concepts eg. unpaid labour, social reproduction, care work, household bargaining etc
Successfully apply key concepts in feminist political economy to historical and contemporary case examples
Actively contribute to class discussion and demonstrate capacity to evaluate and respond constructively to different viewpoints
Prepare written material to a high academic standard that demonstrates independent critical thought and research skills.

units.name: Theories in Political Economy
units.description: This unit seeks to develop a deeper understanding of the various theoretical frameworks within which political economic analysis is constructed, and to which you have been introduced in other political economy units. To do this, you will focus on the methodologies, core concepts and philosophical underpinnings of the principal schools of economic thought with particular emphasis on the non-neoclassical approaches to the study of economic issues. If you are considering further study in political economy (Honours, MPhil or PhD), you are strongly encouraged to undertake this unit as it provides the necessary fundamental preparation for further study.

accessConditions.prerequisite: 12 credit points at 2000 level in Political Economy

learningOutcomes: understand different theories of political economy
apply theories and concepts to study specific issues
make links between economic and political questions
construct a sound argument based on evidence and communicate this effectively (both verbally and in writing)
examine critically received ideas and existing institutions.

units.name: Advanced Theory in Political Economy
units.description: This is an advanced unit in the theoretical foundations of political economy which extends and deepens your knowledge gained from ECOP3911 and complements your studies in ECOP4012. You will interrogate the main schools of critical scholarship, and how they can be deployed in our research practice to illuminate and advance new understandings of contemporary issues in political economy. This will assist your choice of the theoretical framework for your Honours thesis, and inform your knowledge of appropriate application of methodologies as you construct the research project for this thesis.
learningOutcomes: understand theories in political economy that are integral to the study of capitalism
demonstrate a capacity to critically reflect on and evaluate these debates
apply key conceptual ideas to analyse the political economy of inequality
participate in all aspects of the unit of study including class presentations and discussions and independent study
write original and well-researched pieces of work in which you articulate your own unique position and effectively argue your case.

units.name: Political Economy Honours Thesis 1
units.description: This unit is designed to support the development of a student research theses. The unit will include a number of thesis development workshops including an orientation to the honours year, writing a literature review and Research in Progress presentations to a departmental forum. These activities are designed to supplement the regular student-supervisor relationship and thesis writing undertaken in Semester 1.
learningOutcomes: write a research proposal and develop a plan to complete a 20,000-word thesis.

units.name: Political Economy Honours Thesis 2
units.description: This unit requires you to complete an original piece of largely self-directed original research in political economy which you will write up as a 20,000-word thesis. You will be provided with expert supervision by an academic member of the Department of Political Economy who will provide guidance about your research and the thesis writing process.
learningOutcomes: complete a 20,000-word thesis based largely on self-directed, original research.

units.name: Intermediate Microeconomics
units.description: The aim of this unit is the development of theoretical and applied skills in economics. It looks at a variety of decisions made by consumers and producers as they interact in the markets for goods and services, and at the different market structures in which consumers and producers operate. A wide range of topics deepens the understanding of the microeconomics of consumer and producer interaction, including the economics of information and choice under uncertainty; industry structures other than monopoly and perfect competition; general equilibrium and economic efficiency; market failure and the role of government.

accessConditions.prerequisite: ECON1001 or BUSS1040 or ECON1040

learningOutcomes: demonstrate familiarity with the main microeconomic models describing consumer choice and firm behaviour
identify the likely outcome arising from the interaction of firms and consumers
demonstrate understanding of microeconomic concepts and apply analytical models to describe real-world economic situations
demonstrate understanding of the limitations of various models, distinguish between competing explanations of market behaviour, and critically evaluate competing theories
communicate effectively the results of economic analysis and participate in public policy discussions arising in business and government environments.

units.name: Intermediate Macroeconomics
units.description: This unit of study develops models of the goods, money and labour markets, and examines issues in macroeconomic policy. Macroeconomic relationships, covering consumption, investment, money and employment, are explored in detail. Macro-dynamic relationships, especially those linking inflation and unemployment, are also considered. Exchange rates and open economy macroeconomics are also addressed. In the last part of the unit, topics include the determinants and theories of economic growth, productivity and technology, the dynamics of the business cycle, counter-cyclical policy and the relationship between micro and macro policy in the context of recent Australian experience.

accessConditions.prerequisite: ECON1002 or ECON1040

learningOutcomes: Understand theoretical models that form the body of contemporary macroeconomics
Understand and apply macroeconomic models to various economic problems and policy issues
Understand the associated empirical implications of policy issues
Apply new ways of thinking and appreciate the importance of intellectual curiosity and reflection as foundation for continuous learning
Identify, define and analyse problems and recommend creative solutions within real-world constraints
Demonstrate a capacity to work independently including the ability to plan and achieve goals
Critically evaluate underlying theories, concepts, assumptions, limitations and arguments in disciplinary and cross-disciplinary fields of study

units.name: Money and Banking
units.description: Students will learn how a modern financial system operates and the relationships between the financial system and the economy, with a particular emphasis on understanding business cycles. We will study how money/capital changes hands between agents over time, both directly and through institutions. We will study how these exchanges affect the economy, and how central banks and other policy institutions monitor, influence and regulate these exchanges. There will be an equal emphasis on understanding the modern financial system and on analysing monetary policy and financial regulation.

accessConditions.prerequisite: (ECON1001 and ECON1002) or (ECON1040 and ECON1002) or BUSS1040

learningOutcomes: Explain various components of financial markets (bonds, stocks, money, capital, etc.) in channelling funds from lenders/savers to borrowers/investors, either directly or indirectly.
Define fundamental concepts of “money” and “interest” within financial markets and wider economies.
Compare and interpret key money functions, various levels of money aggregates and other monetary variables.
Examine the history of money and distinguish its evolutionary nature across monetary institutions, financial products, and innovations.
Analyse the inter-connections between money, interest rate, intermediary financial institutions (e.g., commercial banks), and the greater economy.
Apply the principles of demand and supply analysis and main monetary theories in financial markets and explain the behaviour of key variables (e.g., interest rate, inflation, aggregate output, etc).
Evaluate and criticise the actions of central banks (or reserve banks), the monetary policies, and their impacts on commercial banks and the wider economy.

units.name: Indigenous Economics and Public Policy
units.description: Australia's Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people had distinctive economic and social systems that were disrupted by European settlement. This unit examines the historical consequences of European settlement for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people through the lens of economics. It introduces students to policy analysis in the Indigenous context and explores the interface between conventional and Indigenous economics. Topics covered include economic history and the impacts of colonialism, inequality, policy applications to contemporary problems and Indigenous economics: rational and relational man in the natural environment.

accessConditions.prerequisite: ECON1001 or ECON1040 or BUSS1040

learningOutcomes: analyse current economic outcomes of Indigenous Australians in their historical context;
demonstrate an understanding of the policy process;
identify insights from Indigenous communities in policy making;
apply theoretical principles in application of Indigenous policy making; and
compare Indigenous economics with standard economic theory.

units.name: East Asian Economies
units.description: This unit of study analyses the economic experiences and policies of key East Asian countries with significant economic ties with Australia. The unit will first introduce how some of these countries achieved the miraculous post-war economic growth and analyse their growth success using economic models. The unit identifies the key issues and challenges facing these countries in both social and global contexts. Emphasis will be placed on the bilateral and multilateral economic relations of East Asian countries with Australia.

accessConditions.prerequisite: ECON1001 or ECON1002 or BUSS1040 or ECON1040

learningOutcomes: develop the key conceptual frameworks necessary for understanding East Asian economic growth
demonstrate understanding of the historical backgrounds and initial conditions that shaped the current East Asian economies
apply economic models for analysing historical and contemporary economic outcomes and policies of East Asia
identify current challenges and opportunities East Asian economies pose.
evaluate current and past policies with critical perspectives

units.name: Applications of Economic Policy
units.description: This unit develops the theoretical framework for the economic analysis of policy interventions by government. Throughout the unit, emphasis is placed on understanding the differential welfare implications of government decisions across populations. A critical skill in the policy development process is the need to design and assess the implications of economic policy under asymmetric information. The role of institutional constraints on real-world economic policy decisions will also be considered. Policy decisions examined will be drawn from a range of contexts, including health, education, and the environment.

accessConditions.prerequisite: (ECON1001 or ECON1040 or BUSS1040) and ECMT1010

learningOutcomes: explain why governments intervene in markets, including concepts of market failure, equity, and efficiency
apply an analytical framework to real policy issues
interpret tables, graphs, and descriptive statistics to draw conclusions about policy outcomes
interpret regression output to assess causal claims and policy impacts
communicate an analysis of a policy problem.

units.name: Intermediate Financial Economics
units.description: This unit introduces micro- and macroeconomic models central for understanding the functioning of financial markets. Models of intertemporal choice and investment decisions provide a foundation for an understanding of asset pricing. The role financial institutions, regulators and money in explaining economic growth and the business cycle are examined.

accessConditions.prerequisite: (ECON1001 or ECON1040 or BUSS1040) and (ECMT1010 or ((MATH1005 or MATH1905) and MATH1115) or DATA1001 or DATA1901 or ENVX1002 or BUSS1020)
accessConditions.prohibition: ECOS2001 or ECOS2901 or ECOS2002 or ECOS2902

learningOutcomes: demonstrate understanding of the main microeconomic models describing consumer choice
identify the likely outcome arising from the interaction of consumers in the market
understand and apply macroeconomic models to various economic problems, financial markets, and policy issues
critically evaluate underlying economic theories, concepts, assumptions, limitations, and arguments and distinguish between competing theories
communicate effectively the results of economic analysis and participate in public policy discussions arising in relation to financial markets.

units.name: Economics of Competition and Strategy
units.description: This unit introduces new and comprehensive methods for the analysis and formation of business strategy. The unit analyses strategies for developing competitive advantages, including product differentiation, cost advantages and product life cycles; implementing incentives, control, firm boundaries, and internal firm decision-making mechanisms; implementing pricing, auction and signalling practices; assessing industry attractiveness and the regulatory/trade practices environment; and managing industry cooperation and conflict. Students are taught a set of tools that they can bring to bear on new problems. Understanding competitive dynamics and strategic thinking are emphasised. Case studies and problem-solving form an important part of the teaching method.

accessConditions.prerequisite: ECON1001 or BUSS1040 or ECON1040

learningOutcomes: acquire the necessary skills to design and analyse business strategies
develop problem-solving skills
develop written communication skills
employ technologies effectively in gathering information from written, oral, and electronic sources
acquire the ability to manage, analyse, evaluate, and use information efficiently and effectively.

units.name: The European Economy
units.description: What economic challenges and opportunities does Europe face? This unit analyses Europe's economic framework and policy experience, its economic institutions and the unique relationship European countries have with each other and the rest of the world. Particular attention is paid to the unique constraints that European policymakers face. This unit provides a practical understanding of European economic management for those who may encounter Europe while working in the private or public sectors. No prior knowledge of Economics is required.

accessConditions.prerequisite: 12 credit points at 1000 level

learningOutcomes: Demonstrate understanding of the economic backgrounds and major events that have shaped the current European Union
Apply economic concepts for analysing and evaluating the European economic policies
Appreciate similarities and differences across the countries that belong to the European Union
Identify the challenges ahead for the EU
Understand the economic interdependence between the EU and other world economies
Identify the costs and benefits of the EU membership
Understand the European decision making within the EU

Understand the economic arguments behind Europe’s common currency project and appreciate the attendant difficulties and opportunities that the Euro has created for policymakers at national and supra-national level
Understand how economic concerns have shaped social policies in the European Union
Understand the economic reasoning behind European integration
Critically analyse events related to the European economy

units.name: Intermediate Microeconomics Honours
units.description: ECOS2901 Intermediate Microeconomics Honours is the first unit of study in the microeconomics sequence in the Advanced Economics Program. ECOS2901 develops theoretical skills in economics that are foundational to all economic modelling. It covers applications and extensions of the theory of consumer choice, firm behaviour, market structure and complete information game theory. These topics are taught with greater detail than in ECOS2001, with more extensions and applications, and require deeper analytical, critical and technical understanding.

accessConditions.prerequisite: Minimum of 70% in (ECON1001 or BUSS1040 or ECON1040)
accessConditions.assumedKnowledge: ECOS2903 or MATH2070 or MATH2970

learningOutcomes: demonstrate knowledge of the main microeconomic models describing consumer choice and firm behaviour
identify the likely outcome arising from the interaction of firms and consumers
demonstrate understanding of microeconomic concepts through analytical models to describe real-world economic situations
identify the limitations of various models, distinguish between competing explanations of market behaviour, and critically evaluate competing theories
communicate effectively the results of economic analysis and participate in public policy discussions arising in business and government environments.

units.name: Intermediate Macroeconomics Honours
units.description: ECOS2902 is part of the macroeconomics sequence in the Advanced Economics Program. The unit is based on ECOS2002 Intermediate Macroeconomics but offers a more advanced treatment of topics. Topics covered include: growth, business cycles, and policy (monetary and fiscal) analysis.

accessConditions.prerequisite: Minimum of 70% in (ECON1002 or ECON1040)

learningOutcomes: demonstrate an understanding of the basic principles and theories of economics
analyse and interpret economic, commercial and business information from diverse sources using economic and econometric models
select and utilise relevant techniques and principles to analyse economic events
compile and present relevant commercial information to decision makers using appropriate data management and IT tools.

units.name: Mathematical Economics
units.description: This unit provides an introduction to mathematical concepts and techniques commonly employed by economists. Topics include: sets, single- and multi-variable functions, continuity, concavity and convexity, differentiation and integration, matrix algebra, unconstrained and constrained optimisation.

accessConditions.prerequisite: Minimum of 70% in (ECON1001 or BUSS1040 or ECON1040 or ECON1002)

learningOutcomes: develop problem-solving skills
construct logical arguments and proofs
Acquire the standard mathematical language to describe and analyse economic problems
acquire the necessary mathematical skills to critically evaluate current research in economics and be in a position to contribute to current research

units.name: Development Economics
units.description: This unit examines the economic transformation of less-developed countries from microeconomic and macroeconomic perspectives. It covers applied topics such as education, health, nutrition, demographics, labour, agriculture and the private sector, focusing on how policies attempt to overcome market and institutional failures that are particularly acute in the developing world. Focus is given to applying theoretical and empirical tools necessary to conceptualise, analyse and interpret various issues in economic development. Applied examples from developing countries are used throughout the unit.

accessConditions.prerequisite: ECOS2001 or ECOS2901 or ECOS2002 or ECOS2902

learningOutcomes: Analyse key microeconomic theories and concepts in development economics to explain poverty, inequality, and economic development outcomes.
Apply simple microeconomic models to analyse development problems and derive testable predictions about behaviour, markets, and policy interventions.
Evaluate empirical strategies used in development economics, including randomized controlled trials and quasi-experimental designs, with attention to identification, validity, and external relevance.
Interpret quantitative and qualitative evidence from development data and research studies to draw defensible conclusions about development policies and interventions.
Critically assess development policies and interventions by integrating economic theory, empirical evidence, and contextual constraints.
Communicate rigorous economic arguments about development issues clearly and persuasively in written form, tailored to academic and policy-oriented audiences.

units.name: Hierarchies, Incentives and Firm Structure
units.description: This unit deals with the coordination and motivation problems faced by firms. More specifically this unit examines: whether firms use price or command mechanisms to allocate resources within firms; the problems associated with designing incentive contracts; the principles of efficient contract design and; the real world applications of those principles. The final section deals with the manner in which the coordination and motivation problems faced by firms determines their financial, vertical and horizontal structure.

accessConditions.prerequisite: ECOS2001 or ECOS2901

learningOutcomes: demonstrate an understanding of important economic factors that help shape the structure of the firm
analyse the way an organisation allocates its decision-making rights, the way it rewards its employees and the measures it uses to assess performance are all interrelated

understand the concepts of: freeriding; principal agent; incentive compatibility; individual rationality constraint; real and formal authority; prisoners’ dilemma; coordination game; and multitask problems, and be able to apply these concepts to real problems faced by organisations

critically evaluate the effect of changes in technology, product market competition and globalisation on these decisions about the internal structure of the businesses, not only from the perspective of the firm (attempting to maximise profit), but also from the perspective of a policy maker (attempting to maximise social welfare).

units.name: History of Economic Thought
units.description: Where do the current beliefs - theories, doctrines, postulates and attitudes - of modern economics come from? If current theories and doctrines have a definite historical beginning, what schools of thought did they supplant? Are there alternative or dissident views which subsisted alongside mainstream economics in the twentieth century - and if so, what are they and where did they originate from? This unit seeks to answer these questions, as well as others. It provides an overview of the development of economic ideas from the seventeenth to the twentieth century, combined with a more intensive focus on the thought of certain key figures in that history. The particular topics covered include: the formation of economics to 1776; Adam Smith; classical economics from Smith to J.S. Mill; the rise of marginalist economics; John Maynard Keynes; and orthodox and heterodox currents in twentieth century economics.

accessConditions.prerequisite: ECOS2001 or ECOS2901 or ECOS2002 or ECOS2902 or ECOP2011 or ECOP2001 or ECOP2012 or ECOP2002

learningOutcomes: attain a deep knowledge of the historical development of the economics discipline
use conceptual systems of thought for analysis and diagnosis
demonstrate a critical understanding of the conceptual machinery of economic thought and analysis
develop effective communication skills, both writing skills and in oral presentation and exchange
demonstrate skills for the appropriation of knowledge to one's self

units.name: Industrial Organisation
units.description: This unit of study examines the nature of inter-firm rivalry in industries with market power. It explores the various ways in which firms can increase their market power by: extracting more surplus from consumers, by colluding with rivals or by excluding entrants. The unit also analyses the international competitiveness of industries in the context of industry assistance and the prevalence of foreign multinationals. Competition policy is also discussed.

accessConditions.prerequisite: ECOS2001 or ECOS2901

learningOutcomes: Understand how markets allocate and generate surplus
Understand the role of the firm in the economic system and analyse what determines the boundaries of a firm
Use economic models to critically analyse the relationship between market structure and market outcomes
Use game theoretic tools to analyse firm strategy concerning output and pricing decisions
Make use of appropriate economic models, analyse firm behaviour in dynamic scenarios (that is, timing of actions is important)
Critically evaluate the role of government in addressing potential market failures and regulating markets.

units.name: International Trade
units.description: This unit of study provides a systematic analysis of the theory of international trade and trade policy. Initially differences between countries are emphasised as the source of trade and the gains from trade. Models that are examined include the Classical-Ricardian model, the Heckscher-Ohlin model and the Specific-Factors model. Next economics of scale and imperfect competition are introduced as sources of trade and gains from trade. The unit concludes with an examination of empirical studies aimed at testing trade theories. The analysis of trade policy begins with a discussion of the instruments of trade policy, in particular, tariffs and quotas and their effect on welfare. This discussion is then extended to the case of imperfect competition and strategic trade policy.

accessConditions.prerequisite: ECOS2001 or ECOS2901

learningOutcomes: demonstrate skills in oral and written communication
demonstrate skills in problem solving
develop proficiency in critical thinking
demonstrate basic modelling skills
identify and intuitively explain the key issues in international trade theory and policy such as, for example, the impact of trade on efficiency and welfare
understand the importance of assumptions in the economic modelling of international trade
distinguish between the efficiency implications and distributional consequences of trade and trade policy
understand the role of politics in trade and vice versa
assess the costs and benefits of trade policy from an economic point of view
confidently participate in public policy discussions and be ready to challenge some of the misconceptions regarding trade and globalisation.

units.name: International Macroeconomics
units.description: This unit explores macroeconomic theory and policy in an open economy context, emphasising the interconnectedness of global markets. It examines the microfoundations of key economic sectors and their implications for international macroeconomic dynamics. Topics covered include, but are not limited to, foreign exchange markets, interest rate parity, exchange rate determination and intervention, the goods and money markets, and the international monetary system. The unit also analyses the role of policymakers and the effects of monetary, fiscal, and other macroeconomic policies on both small and large open economies under different exchange rate regimes.

accessConditions.prerequisite: ECOS2002 or ECOS2902 or ECOS2040

learningOutcomes: demonstrate openness to new ways of thinking and appreciate the importance of intellectual curiosity and reflection as the foundation for continuous learning
demonstrate a capacity to work independently
critically evaluate underlying theories, concepts, assumptions, limitations and arguments in economics
develop coherent arguments when recommending solutions and critically evaluating theories in economics
understand the theoretical models that form the body of contemporary international macroeconomics
understand and apply international macroeconomic models to various economic problems and issues
understand the associated empirical implications and policy issues

units.name: Labour Economics
units.description: This unit aims to provide an understanding of labour markets and related issues such as work conditions, pay and employment levels. Labour supply and demand, theories of wage determination, labour mobility and discrimination are examined. It also analyses the role of trade unions and labour market contracts. These topics are applied to current issues in Australian labour markets such as enterprise bargaining, the role of centralised wage fixing systems, training and other labour market programs. Policies designed to improve the functioning of the labour market are examined and particular attention is given to the problem of persistent unemployment.

accessConditions.prerequisite: ECOS2001 or ECOS2901

learningOutcomes: Understand the particular issues involved in conducting empirical research;
Understand the economic concepts, theories, and methods used in the study of labour economics;
Apply appropriate economic tools to analyse decision-making underlying the supply and demand of labour;
Evaluate the theories and concepts used in labour economics;
Understand the main econometric issues and empirical techniques used in analysing labour market data and in evaluating alternative theories;
Develop and present coherent arguments on current issues in labour markets and labour market policies;
Demonstrate problem-solving and critical-thinking skills;
Develop an ethical awareness in analysing data and reporting results;
Evaluate ideas, views, and evidence

units.name: Monetary Economics
units.description: This unit provides an overview of the main elements of monetary economics, with emphasis upon macroeconomic issues - analysis of economic processes in which money enters the picture in an essential manner. The content primarily concerns economic principles and theory, but there is also considerable focus on the Australian monetary system and monetary policy in particular. The particular topics covered include: functions of money; the concept of 'liquidity'; money demand; determinants of money supply changes; financial crises and the 'lender of last resort' function of central banking; the Reserve Bank of Australia and the Australian Prudential Regulation Authority; term and risk structures of interest rates; alternative theories of the level of the rate of interest; the monetary policy transmission mechanism; monetary policy instrument choice; central bank credibility; policy reaction functions; the global monetary system; and Reserve Bank market operations.

accessConditions.prerequisite: ECOS2001 or ECOS2901 or ECOS2002 or ECOS2902 or ECOS2040

learningOutcomes: identify, define and analyse problems and your solutions in monetary economics
conduct economic research using libraries, the web and other sources of information
negotiate and create shared understandings by respectfully interacting with others
demonstrate a capacity for openness to new ways of thinking and appreciation of the importance of intellectual curiosity and reflection as a foundation for continuous learning.

units.name: Public Finance
units.description: Public finance is about the taxing and spending decisions of governments. This unit covers a wide range of public finance topics. After an introduction to welfare economics and the role of government in the economy, the unit focuses on the revenue side of the budget: tax incidence, externalities, efficient and equitable taxation of individuals, and the effects of taxes on corporations. It then focuses on the expenditure side of the government budget: public goods, retirement income policy and programs providing social insurance.

accessConditions.prerequisite: ECOS2001 or ECOS2901

learningOutcomes: apply economic concepts to examine real-world problems from both an individual’s and policymaker’s perspective
demonstrate problem-solving skills
critically evaluate the assumptions and limitations of the theories and arguments presented in class
demonstrate written communication skills
employ technologies effectively in gathering information from written, oral, and electronic sources
manage, analyse, evaluate and use information efficiently and effectively.

units.name: Strategic Behaviour
units.description: To think and act strategically, one needs to evaluate the effect of one's actions on the actions of others. As most economic decisions are strategic, such as the decision to lower a price or introduce a new tax, economics, if it is to avoid simplistic models, requires a theoretical framework capable of illuminating strategic behaviour. This unit offers a comprehensive, critical introduction to the theory which purports, not only to satisfy this theoretical need, but also potentially to unify the social sciences: game theory. After examining important concepts of game theory, the unit investigates the repercussions for the theory of bargaining and for the evolution of social institutions.

accessConditions.prerequisite: ECOS2001 or ECOS2901

learningOutcomes: design optimal strategies and make rational predictions in social and business interactions
examine important concepts of game theory
Apply models of game theory to analyse strategic aspects of real-world interactions
Comprehend individual and institutional behaviours from a rational perspective
Master the necessary mathematical tools for introductory and intermediate game theory

units.name: Environmental Economics
units.description: This unit focuses on the economics of environmental problems and the solutions to those problems. We cover economic sources of environmental problems, including market failures due to externalities and public goods. Policies for addressing environmental problems are then analysed. These include Pigouvian taxes and subsidies; regulation with asymmetric information; tradable permits; regulations for public goods and open-access resources; and the allocation of property rights. Applications to climate change, pollution, valuing the environment, and sustainability, among others, are covered.

accessConditions.prerequisite: AREC2005 or ECOS2001 or ECOS2901

learningOutcomes: present a clear and coherent exposition of economic knowledge, ideas and empirical evidence both orally and in writing, in the context of environmental economics
frame problems in terms of core economic concepts and principles, and apply economic reasoning and analytical skills, in order to make informed judgements and decisions
access data and implement appropriate empirical techniques to interpret the results
explain the nature and implications of assumptions and value judgements in economics.

units.name: Law and Economics
units.description: Law and economics examines the economic role of law and legal institutions on the actions of economic agents. The economic analysis of law is founded on models of human behaviour and examines how decision making is affected by different legal regimes. The behavioral approach gives rise to a set of principles that can be applied widely across disparate areas of the law, and is becoming increasingly important world-wide, as such analysis is often utilized in courts and public policy forums. The unit begins with a revision of relevant tools of economic analysis. Subsequently, it studies the economics of various branches of law such as: property; contract; nuisance; accident and liability law; and, criminal law

accessConditions.prerequisite: ECOS2001 or ECOS2901

learningOutcomes: Demonstrate an understanding of economic concepts and reasoning when examining the effect of legal rules
Demonstrate problem-solving skills in the application of economics to law and legal institutions
Communicate how the principles of economics can be used to analyse the law and legal institutions
Undertake individual scholarly research on aspects of law and economics.

units.name: Experimental and Behavioural Economics
units.description: Experimental economics uses experimental methods to evaluate the performance of economic models, institutions and policies. Behavioural economics combines experimental and field evidence with insights from neighbouring disciplines such as psychology, to develop richer economic models of decision-making. This unit will develop the key research methods and major findings of each of these fields, and explore both theoretical and practical implications. Students will read a number of seminal research papers in both experimental and behavioural economics, and will have opportunities to participate in classroom experiments.

accessConditions.prerequisite: ECOS2001 or ECOS2901

learningOutcomes: Understand how experimental and behavioural economics relate to other methods and bodies of thought, and in particular to ‘standard’ economic theory
Demonstrate familiarity with the main areas to which experimental and behavioural economics have been applied, and some key findings that have been observed in each of these areas
Recognise the major departures from rationality that are identified in experimental and behavioural economics
Understand how economic theories are being revised in light of experimental and behavioural economics findings
Appreciate how experimental and behavioural economics methods contribute to explaining field phenomena, and the design of policy
Critically review and evaluate original research in experimental and behavioural economics

units.name: Health Economics
units.description: The purpose of this unit is to introduce the student to the methods of health economics and demonstrate how these methods can be applied to analyse issues in health policy and management. This unit will teach the student to use economic analysis to understand critical issues in health care and health policy. Topics covered include the institutions of the Australian system of health care and health statistics, evaluation techniques, production of health, demand for health care and technology, moral hazard and adverse selection in health insurance markets, health labour markets, including physician-patient interactions, managed care, regulation and payment systems for providers, comparative health systems, the pharmaceutical industry, health policy and social insurance.

accessConditions.prerequisite: ECOS2001 or ECOS2901

learningOutcomes: demonstrate problem-solving skills
demonstrate written communication skills
employ technologies effectively in gathering information from written, oral, and electronic sources
manage, analyse, evaluate and use information efficiently and effectively
analyse and understand issues in health economics and policy.

units.name: Economics of Growth
units.description: At the heart of an understanding of the dynamics of market or capitalist economies is an understanding of economic growth. This unit is an introduction to the analysis of economic growth, including a comparison of competing explanations. It considers the connection between growth and distribution, growth and technical progress, the role of economic policies and economic institutions, as well as the limitations on growth associated with exhaustible natural resources. Some consideration of the empirical evidence on different explanations of growth is also provided.

accessConditions.prerequisite: (ECOS2001 or ECOS2901) and (ECOS2002 or ECOS2902)

learningOutcomes: demonstrate openness to new ways of thinking and appreciate the importance of intellectual curiosity and reflection as the foundation for continuous learning
critically evaluate underlying theories, concepts, assumptions, limitations, and arguments in economics.

units.name: Special Topic in Economics 1
units.description: This unit of study consists of a special topic in economics, periodically available through staff research interests and the presence of visiting academic staff. As such, the topic and availability of the unit varies from semester to semester, and students should consult the unit of study outline for details pertinent to their intended semester of enrolment.

accessConditions.prerequisite: (ECOS2001 or ECOS2901) or (ECOS2002 or ECOS2902) or (ECOS2040 and ECMT2130)

learningOutcomes: Interpret and apply core economic concepts relevant to climate change and sustainability.
Design environmental and climate policies using economic frameworks.
Apply economic reasoning to assess climate policy effectiveness.
Evaluate sustainability challenges and trade-offs in addressing them.
Use economic insights to inform judgments about climate policy trade-offs.

units.name: Business Cycles and Asset Markets
units.description: The unit of study provides theoretical and empirical training in analysing macroeconomic fluctuations and the interactions between the real economy and asset markets. The unit of study will introduce theoretical models of the business cycle to identify sources of economic fluctuations. It then provides a theoretical framework in which the asset market-the real economy can be analysed. In addition to theoretical analysis, the unit will develop empirical tools for analysing economic and financial indicators as well as evaluating the performance of theoretical models. The role of government policy will also be discussed by taking both Australian and global episodes.

accessConditions.prerequisite: ((ECOS2001 or ECOS2901) and (ECOS2002 or ECOS2902)) or (ECOS2040 and ECMT2130)

learningOutcomes: explain the business cycle indicators that should be part of every economic analyst’s and decision-maker’s information set
employ empirical or theoretical models for understanding and analysing fluctuations in the aggregate economy and asset prices, while understanding the limitations of the models
assess domestic and global economic conditions using key economic and financial indicators and critically evaluate government policy measures
work with other students cooperatively and responsibly.

units.name: The Economics of Financial Markets
units.description: Financial assets play a vital role in coordinating the actions of investors; consequently, they play a crucial role in creating wealth and facilitating economic activity. This unit provides students with an understanding of the economic foundations of financial theory and the economic framework upon which that theory is based. Much of the work covered is an application of microeconomic theory to the special problems encountered in the study of asset markets and the financial side of an economy. It provides an understanding of the role of financial assets and of the modern approaches to asset pricing theory.

accessConditions.prerequisite: ((ECOS2001 or ECOS2901) and (ECOS2002 or ECOS2902)) or (ECOS2040 and ECMT2130)

learningOutcomes: explain and apply the fundamental principles of asset pricing, including key models and theories
analyse the roles and functions of financial markets in facilitating resource allocation and risk management
critically evaluate theoretical asset pricing models by comparing their predictions to observed market behaviour and stylised facts
develop and demonstrate advanced problem-solving skills in asset pricing through quantitative and analytical methods.

units.name: Personnel Economics
units.description: The management of human resources is key to the success of modern organisations. This unit of study introduces economic concepts and analytical tools that provide a rigorous framework with which to analyse this challenge. Topics covered include the design of compensation schemes to achieve strategic goals; recruitment and hiring decisions; optimal turnover of staff; facilitating teamwork and worker empowerment; and, peer relationships within the modern business organisation.

accessConditions.prerequisite: ECOS2001 or ECOS2901

learningOutcomes: understand the challenges faced by managers within organisations in regards to personnel issues and to develop the skills required to analyse human resource practices using rigorous economic models
apply economic concepts to examine real world problems from the perspective of a manager within an organisation
develop problem solving skills that can be applied to personnel issues within an organisation
critically evaluate the assumptions and limitations of the theories and arguments presented in class
develop written and oral communication skills
apply technologies effectively in gathering information from written, oral, and electronic sources
manage, analyse, evaluate and use information efficiently and effectively
develop a coherent argument and justify the conclusions reached by reference to research

units.name: Economic History
units.description: This unit covers topics in economic history from the advent of European 'modernity' in the 17th century to the late 20th century. A major focus is identifying the main social, institutional and economic forces that explain the unprecedented development of the world economy over the past 300 years. Topics include the first industrial revolution in Britain, the industrialization of Western Europe and the United States, the 1930s Great Depression and recovery, post-World War II reconstruction and 'golden era' of growth, and East Asia's meteoric growth performance.

accessConditions.prerequisite: ECOS2001 or ECOS2901 or ECOS2002 or ECOS2902

learningOutcomes: demonstrate a disciplinary expertise in global economic history since 1066
achieve interdisciplinary effectiveness by setting current global economic issues in historical context
refine critical thinking and problem solving by deepening the understanding of core economic theory principles and tools
improve information and digital literacy by managing, analysing, evaluating and using research materials efficiently and effectively
extend oral and written communication skills through formal assessments and active participation in class

units.name: The Economics of Regulation
units.description: Market outcomes can be undesirable when self-interested firms reduce welfare for consumers and society. This unit of study focuses on the regulation of firms in markets with imperfect competition. We analyse regulation of natural monopolies, focusing on the key issue of asymmetric information between the regulator and the monopolist. In this unit we also examine oligopoly markets in which firms can reduce welfare through collusion, price fixing and vertical restraints. Emphasising real-world examples, we examine competition policy and merger regulation.

accessConditions.prerequisite: ECOS2001 or ECOS2901 or ECOS2040

learningOutcomes: justify regulatory intervention
understand the fundamental trade-offs involved in regulation
understand regulation versus competition policy
apply regulatory economics tools to solve practical policy and industry problems

units.name: Economics of Crime
units.description: This unit of study applies economic concepts and theory to analyse criminal behaviour and its implications for society. Students will critically analyse topics related to the criminal justice system, including policing, incarceration, and punishment. Within an economic framework, we will also consider the role that social programs and other social conditions, such as education and poverty, play in affecting crime. We will apply these key topics to analyse the impacts of new policies and technologies in the criminal justice context.

accessConditions.prerequisite: ECOS2001 or ECOS2901

learningOutcomes: Apply economic concepts to topics in economics of crime
Demonstrate an understanding of insights provided by economics as they apply to real-world problems in economics of crime
Critically evaluate the assumptions and limitations of research papers discussed in class
Develop effective written and oral communication skills in discussing and evaluating research findings
Demonstrate an understanding of the nature and implications of assumptions and value judgements involved in economics research
Participate effectively in class discussions

units.name: Economics of the Family
units.description: This unit applies economic concepts and theory to analyse the family. The unit explores the empirical support for the theories, evaluates explanations for recent demographic and labour market trends, and examines the implications of using the family as the foundation of analysis of economic activity in society. Topics covered include family formation, trends in educational attainment, the changing roles of men and women in the labour market and the household, and the effects of government policies on the family.

accessConditions.prerequisite: ECOS2001 or ECOS2901

learningOutcomes: Apply economic concepts and theory to an analysis of the family
Apply economic concepts to analyse the impact of public policy on family decisions
Apply problem-solving skills to the analysis of the family
Apply technologies effectively in gathering information from written, oral and electronic resources
Rigorously analyse the causes and consequences of decision-making by families, by integrating existing or emerging economic knowledge and data
Develop written and verbal communication skills
